A new approach to the representation theory of the partition category Thanks: Authors supported in part by the National Science Foundation grant DMS-2101783.
Jonathan Brundan, Max Vargas

Abstract
. We explain a new approach to the representation theory of the partition category based on a reformulation of the definition of the Jucys-Murphy elements introduced originally by Halverson and Ram and developed further by Enyang. Our reformulation involves a new graphical monoidal category, the affine partition category , which is defined here as a certain monoidal subcategory of Khovanov’s Heisenberg category. We use the Jucys-Murphy elements to construct some special projective functors, then apply these functors to give self-contained proofs of results of Comes and Ostrik on blocks of Deligne’s category Re ¯ ​ p ​ ( S t ) \underline{\text{Re}}\text{p}(S_{t}) .



2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 18M05; Secondary 20C30, 17B10.

1.
Introduction

Let
\Bbbk
be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero
and
t\in\Bbbk
be a parameter.
The
partition category

\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is the free strict
\Bbbk
-linear symmetric
monoidal category
generated by a special commutative Frobenius object
of categorical dimension
t
. Its additive Karoubi envelope is
the category
\underline{\text{Re}}\text{p}(S_{t})
introduced by Deligne
[
D
]
, which interpolates the categories of representations of the symmetric groups
S_{t}\>(t\in\mathbb{N})
to non-integer values of
t
.
When
t\notin\mathbb{N}
, Deligne’s category is a semisimple tensor category which is not of sub-exponential growth, hence, it does not admit a fiber functor; see
[
EGNO
, Sec. 9.12]
for further background here.
When
t\in\mathbb{N}
, the category
\underline{\text{Re}}\text{p}(S_{t})
is not semisimple,
and its semisimplification is the usual tensor category

\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
of representations of the symmetric group.

The objects of the partition category are indexed by the natural numbers.
For
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
the endomorphism algebra
\End_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n)
is the
partition algebra

P_{n}(t)
introduced by Martin
[
M1
]
and Jones
[
J
]
.
The representation theory of this finite-dimensional algebra
has been well studied. In
[
M2
]
, Martin showed that

P_{n}(t){\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
is a highest weight category except when
t=0
, and he
determined the precise structure of the standard modules; see also
[
DW
]
.
When
t=0
,
P_{n}(t)
still has the structure of a cellular algebra, as established in
[
DW
,
X
]
, and its representation theory is also well understood.
The partition algebras form a tower
P_{0}(t)<P_{1}(t)<\cdots
, but
the cell modules do not restrict along this tower in a multiplicity-free way,
so that standard techniques like the Jones basic construction cannot be applied directly. To address this, Martin
[
M3
]
and Halverson and Ram
[
HR
]

consider
an intermediate family of “half partition algebras” fitting into
a tower

P_{0}(t)<P_{\frac{1}{2}}(t)<P_{1}(t)<P_{\frac{3}{2}}(t)<\cdots.

Halverson and Ram also defined analogs

L_{0},L_{\frac{1}{2}},L_{1},L_{\frac{3}{2}},\dots

of Jucys-Murphy elements in these partition algebras, which were studied further by Enyang
[
E1
,
E2
]
. Enyang
worked out a recursive definition for the Jucys-Murphy elements and
used them to construct an analog of Young’s orthogonal form for the
irreducible
P_{n}(t)
-modules. His definition
involves a complicated
five term recurrence relation, making the Jucys-Murphy elements for partition algebras considerably harder to work with than the classical Jucys-Murphy elements of the symmetric groups.
Recently, Creedon
[
Cr
]
has revisited Enyang’s work,
showing that supersymmetric polynomials in a renormalization of the Jucys-Murphy elements give a family of central elements which is large
enough to separate blocks.

In this article, we give a new treatment of the representation theory of

\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. Let

Par_{t}:=\bigoplus_{m,n\in\mathbb{N}}\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)

be the path algebra of this

\Bbbk
-linear category, denoting the idempotents arising from the identity endomorphisms of the objects of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
by
\{1_{n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}
.
Since the partition algebra
P_{n}(t)

is the idempotent truncation
1_{n}Par_{t}1_{n}
, most of the known results about the representation theory of the algebras
P_{n}(t)
can be deduced
from that of the partition category in a standard way.
In fact, as well as producing more general results, we are convinced that it is
easier to study the representation theory of the partition
category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
, instead of working with the tower of partition algebras.
To start with,
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
has an efficient monoidal presentation encoding its
universal property, with generating morphisms

(“crossing”),

(“merge”),

(“split”),

(“cap”),

(“cup”),

{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ
(“downward leaf”) and

{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ
(“upward leaf”); see
definition

3.1
.
This means that one can make calculations in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
using
the string calculus for strict
monoidal categories, which seems more flexible
than the traditional algebraic expressions used when working in
P_{n}(t)
.
But the key reason we prefer to work with
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is that its
path algebra has a
triangular decomposition
in the sense of
[
BS
, Def. 5.31]
, hence, the category
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
of locally finite-dimensional
Par_{t}
-modules
is an
upper finite highest weight category
as in
[
BS
, Def. 3.34]
.
The Cartan subalgebra in this triangular decomposition is the locally unital algebra

{S\!ym}:=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\Bbbk S_{n},

with its irreducible modules being the Specht modules
\{S(\lambda)\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\}
indexed by the set
\mathcal{P}
of all partitions.
The
standard modules

\{\Delta(\lambda)\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\}

for
Par_{t}
are the modules defined by parabolically inducing the
Specht modules.
Then we obtain a full set of pairwise inequivalent irreducible
Par_{t}
-modules

\{L(\lambda)\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\}
from the irreducible heads of the standard modules. This gives a quick proof of the classification of irreducible
Par_{t}
-modules, which was established originally by Deligne
[
D
]

and Comes and Ostrik
[
CO
]
.

The highest weight
approach to the representation theory of combinatorial monoidal categories such as
the partition category as just outlined
has been developed systematically
by Sam and Snowden
[
SS2
]
. In their language,
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is a

monoidal triangular category
. There are many
other interesting examples of this structure,
including several that are actually monoidal subcategories of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
:
the Brauer category (cups, caps and crossings but no splits and merges),
the Temperley-Lieb category (just cups and caps), and
the category
studied by Khovanov and Sazdanovic in
[
KS
]
(just leaves).
In their earlier work
[
SS1
]
, Sam and Snowden had already
exposed the importance of the structure of the Borel subcategories of these
and other such categories, although at that time
they did not work out the details fully in the case of the partition category.
In
section

3
, we fill this gap by giving an exposition
of some of their ideas in this case, exploiting the structure of the
upper partition category
, i.e., the positive Borel subcategory,
to determine the Grothendieck ring
K_{0}(Par_{t})
of the
category of finitely generated projective
Par_{t}
-modules.
In fact, as a ring, this is identified with the ring
\Lambda
of symmetric functions, but the isomorphism classes of the standard modules
\Delta(\lambda)

produce an interesting inhomogeneous
basis
\{\tilde{s}_{\lambda}\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\}
for

\Lambda
of
deformed Schur functions
.
These also appeared implicitly in
[
D
,
CO
]
and again in
[
SS1
]
, and
were rediscovered from a slightly different perspective by
Orellana and Zabrocki
[
OZ
]
. They are interesting because the structure constants for multiplication in
\Lambda
with respect to this basis are the
reduced Kronecker coefficients
.

Although
there are many important examples of monoidal triangular categories,
and the work of Sam and Snowden has revealed many common features, this still seems to be a subject where the more intricate combinatorics needs to be studied
separately in each case. For example, one wants to understand the
center
of the underlying category, and the induced
decomposition of the irreducible representations into blocks which comes from considering central characters. This can be framed as a question about
an analog of
Harish-Chandra homomorphism
for monoidal triangular categories; see
section

5.1
.
However, to answer it,
one needs some way to construct sufficiently many central elements, and we do not know any uniform way to approach this.
After understanding the block decomposition, the next step is to
consider the combinatorics of

special
projective functors
, which are functors on the module category induced by tensoring with generating objects of the underlying monoidal category.

The crucial new ingredient in our approach to
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

is the definition of another graphical monoidal category, the
affine partition category

\mathpzc{APar}
.
This is obtained from the partition category by adjoining two new generating morphisms

\bullet
(“left dot”)
and

\bullet
(“right dot”) in such a way that

\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
can be recovered as the quotient of
\mathpzc{APar}
by a
certain left tensor ideal, with the left and right dots mapping to
renormalized versions of the Jucys-Murphy elements; see
theorems

4.15
and
4.19
.
However, it is not easy to do this without making additional choices.
The actual definition of
\mathpzc{APar}

given in
definition

4.6
below adopts a quite different point of view
based on an observation due to Likeng and Savage
[
LSR
]
: we construct

\mathpzc{APar}
initially as a
monoidal subcategory of Khovanov’s Heisenberg category
\mathpzc{Heis}
from
[
K
]
.
This allows complicated relations in
\mathpzc{APar}
to be derived
rather quickly by elementary calculations using
the string calculus for
\mathpzc{Heis}
; e.g., see
lemma

4.10

which recovers
Enyang’s five term recurrence relation for the Jucys-Murphy elements.

In the affine partition category, there is an obvious way to
construct a large family of central elements; see
theorem

4.23
.
These map to central elements in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
which turn out to be closely related to Creedon’s central elements of the partition algebras from
[
Cr
]
.
After that, we consider the self-adjoint projective functor

D:Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod}}

induced by tensoring with the generating object
1
of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
.
This plays an analogous role in our approach to induction and restriction
along the tower of partition algebras in the work of Martin and others discussed earlier.
We use the action of the left and right dots from
\mathpzc{APar}
to decompose
D

into summands

D=\bigoplus_{a,b\in\Bbbk}D_{b|a}
; see
theorem

5.18
. There is
a close analogy here to the way Jucys-Murphy elements were used to give a
new approach to the representation theory of the symmetric groups in
[
OV
]
.
In fact, the Jucys-Murphy elements of
Par_{t}
generate a large commutative subalgebra, and the resulting “Gelfand-Tsetlin characters” of the standard modules

\Delta(\lambda)
can be computed explicitly using the branching rules from

theorem

5.18
, although we do not pursue this further here.
Finally, we use the combinatorial properties of the special projective functors

D_{b|a}
to reprove the main structural result
about the representation theory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
for
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
This was established originally by Comes and Ostrik
[
CO
]
.

Theorem.

When
t\in\mathbb{N}
, i.e.,
Par_{t}
is not semisimple,
the non-simple blocks of
Par_{t}

are in bijection with isomorphism classes of irreducibles in
the semisimplification

\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
.
All of the non-simple blocks are Morita equivalent. These blocks have
infinitely many isomorphism classes of irreducible modules
parametrized by
\mathbb{N}
, and the structure of the corresponding indecomposable
projectives is as follows:

.

This quiver
is well known in representation theory, for example,
it also describes the non-trivial block of the Temperley-Lieb category, as noted in
[
CO
, Rem. 6.5]
.

It is interesting to compare the general strategy
developed here with the original arguments of Comes and Ostrik. There are many parallels. For example, they also construct a large family of central elements, although different from ours, and they also use summands of the functor
D
to construct equivalences between blocks; see
remark

4.27
and
theorem

5.21
.
Another technique which is crucial in
[
CO
]

is the idea of lifting projectives
to the (semisimple) generic partition category. In our approach, this
is replaced everywhere with arguments involving standard modules
and the BGG reciprocity coming from the highest weight structure. In fact,
largely due to the fact that they did not think in these module-theoreic terms, Comes and Ostrik were forced in the end to refer to some of Martin’s results from
[
M2
]
to obtain the precise submodule structure of projectives in the above theorem, whereas our proof is independent of
loc. cit.
, indeed, Martin’s results can now be deduced from here.
One more key idea used by Comes and Ostrik involves
an explicit formula for categorical dimensions derived ultimately from the hook
formula, although we have avoided such considerations entirely
by exploiting the functors
D_{b|a}
for
a=b
.
The definition of these diagonal components of
D
cannot be formulated without using
Jucys-Murphy elements, so
no counterpart for this part of our argument appears in
[
CO
]
.

We thank Alistair Savage for discussions which influenced
the final form of the definition of the affine partition category
given in
definition

4.6
.

2.
Monoidal categories and representations

In the opening section, we explain our general conventions for
representations of
\Bbbk
-linear (monoidal) categories.
Always in this article
\Bbbk
will be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, although all of the generalities recorded
make sense more generally. Then we briefly recall some
classical results about
\mathpzc{Sym}
, the free strict
\Bbbk
-linear symmetric monoidal category on one object, which categorifies the ring of symmetric functions.

2.1.
Path algebras and modules

Let
\mathpzc{A}
be a
\Bbbk
-linear category.
Its
path algebra
is
the associative algebra

A:=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\operatorname{ob}\mathpzc{A}}\Hom_{\mathpzc{A}}(X,Y)

with multiplication induced by composition in
\mathpzc{A}
, so that
gf=g\circ f

for
f:X\rightarrow Y,\ g:Y\rightarrow Z
.
Note that
A
is not necessarily unital, but it is always
a
locally unital algebra
, i.e., there is a distinguished family

\{1_{X}\>|\>X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}\}
of mutually orthogonal idempotents such that

A=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{Y}A1_{X}
. In this case,
\mathbb{O}_{A}
is
the object set
\operatorname{ob}\mathpzc{A}
of the
category
\mathpzc{A}
, with
1_{X}
being the identity endomorphism of
X
.
If
\mathpzc{A}
is a
finite-dimensional category
, i.e., its morphism spaces
are finite-dimensional, then the path algebra is
locally finite-dimensional

in the sense that
\dim 1_{Y}A1_{X}<\infty

for all
X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
.

The category
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
of left
A
-modules is the category

\HOM_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A},\mathpzc{Vec})
of
\Bbbk
-linear functors from
\mathpzc{A}
to the category
\mathpzc{Vec}
of vector spaces, morphisms being natural transformations.
Equivalently, using the language we systematically adopt below,
a left
A
-module
V
is a left module in the usual sense of associative algebras such that
V=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}V
;
this corresponds to the
\Bbbk
-linear functor
V:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Vec}

taking object
X
to the vector space
V(X)=1_{X}V

and morphism
f\in\Hom{A}(X,Y)
to the linear map

V(f):1_{X}V\rightarrow 1_{Y}V
defined by left multiplication by
f\in 1_{Y}A1_{X}
.
There is also the category
{\operatorname{Mod-}}A
of right
A
-modules, which is just the same as the
category
\HOM_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A}^{\operatorname{op}},\mathpzc{Vec})
.

We say that
V\in A{\operatorname{-Mod}}

is
locally finite-dimensional
if
\dim 1_{X}V<\infty

for all
X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
; equivalently, the associated functor goes from

\mathpzc{A}
to the category
\mathpzc{Vec}_{\operatorname{fd}}
of finite-dimensional vector spaces.
Let
A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
be the full subcategory of
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
consisting of the locally finite-dimensional
A
-modules.
For more background material about the structure of the category
A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}

in the case that
A
is locally finite-dimensional, we refer to

[
BS
,
\lx@sectionsign
2.2–
\lx@sectionsign
2.3]
, where Abelian categories of this form are called

Schurian categories
.

We also let
A{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
be the full subcategory of
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}

consisting of the
globally finite-dimensional modules, i.e., the
V
with
\dim V<\infty
,
and
A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
be the full subcategory of
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
consisting of the finitely generated projective modules. If
A
is a locally finite-dimensional locally unital algebra
then
A1_{X}
is a locally finite-dimensional module for each
X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
,
hence,
A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
is a subcategory of
A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
.
The category
A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
can also be obtained in equivalent form directly from the

\Bbbk
-linear category
\mathpzc{A}
since
the Yoneda embedding
h^{*}:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\HOM_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A},\mathpzc{Vec})

induces a contravariant
\Bbbk
-linear equivalence between

\Kar(\mathpzc{A})
and

A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
. Here,
\Kar(\mathpzc{A})
denotes the

additive Karoubi envelope
of
\mathpzc{A}
, that is, the idempotent completion of its additive envelope
\operatorname{Add}(\mathpzc{A})
.

We let
K_{0}(A)
be the split Grothendieck group of the category
A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
. Assuming that
A
is
locally finite-dimensional, every finitely generated module
has a projective cover in
A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
. Moreover,

K_{0}(A)
is a free Abelian group with
canonical
basis coming from the projective covers of the irreducible
A
-modules.

2.2.
Pull-back and push-forward

Suppose that
\mathpzc{A}
and
\mathpzc{B}
are two
\Bbbk
-linear categories.
Let

A=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{Y}A1_{X},\qquad B=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{B}}1_{Y}B1_{X}

be their path algebras.
To a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
F:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{B}
,
we associate an exact
functor

(2.1)

\res_{F}:B{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod}}

which we call
restriction along
F
.
It is just the functor
\HOM_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{B},\mathpzc{Vec})\rightarrow\HOM_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A},\mathpzc{Vec})

defined by composing on the right with
F
.
In elementary terms, and introducing a shorthand which will be ubiquitous later on, the functor

\res_{F}
takes
V\in B{\operatorname{-Mod}}
to

(2.2)

1_{F}V:=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{FX}V\in A{\operatorname{-Mod}},

with the left module structure defined so that
f\in 1_{Y}A1_{X}
acts on the

X
-th summand
1_{FX}V
as
the linear map
Ff:1_{FX}V\rightarrow 1_{FY}V
, and it acts as zero on all other summands.
It takes a
B
-module homomorphism
\phi:V\rightarrow W
to the

A
-module homomorphism
\res_{F}(\phi):1_{F}V\rightarrow 1_{F}W

defined by
\phi_{FX}:1_{FX}V\rightarrow 1_{FX}W

for each
X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
.
Similarly, there is the exact restriction functor we denote by

(2.3)

{{}_{F}\!}\res:{\operatorname{Mod-}}B\rightarrow{\operatorname{Mod-}}A

between the categories of right modules taking
V\in{\operatorname{Mod-}}B
to

(2.4)

V1_{F}:=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}V1_{FX}\in{\operatorname{Mod-}}A.

The functors
\res_{F}
and
{{}_{F}\!}\res
may also be denoted

F^{*}
and
(F^{\operatorname{op}})^{*}
; e.g., see

[
SS1
, (2.1.4)]
,
[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
3.6]
.

The restriction
B1_{F}=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}B1_{FX}

is a
(B,A)
-bimodule.
The functor
\res_{F}:B{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
is isomorphic to

\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}\Hom_{B}(B1_{FX},?)
. Then adjointness of tensor and hom in the locally unital setting (e.g., see
[
BS
, Lem. 2.7]
) implies that the functor

(2.5)

\ind_{F}:=B1_{F}\otimes_{A}:A{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow B{\operatorname{-Mod}}

is left adjoint to
\res_{F}
. We call this
induction along

F
.
Since it is left adjoint to an exact functor,
\ind_{F}
is right exact and takes projectives to
projectives. In fact, we have that

(2.6)

\ind_{F}\;A1_{X}=B1_{F}\otimes_{A}A1_{X}\cong B1_{FX},

i.e.,
\ind_{F}
can be viewed as an extension of
F
to
arbitrary modules.
From this, it is clear that
\ind_{F}
preserves finite generation.
Likewise, the restriction
1_{F}B=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{FX}B
is an
(A,B)
-bimodule.
The functor
\res_{F}
is also isomorphic to
1_{F}B\otimes_{B}
, hence, it has a right adjoint given by the functor

(2.7)

\coind_{F}:=\bigoplus_{Y\in\mathbb{O}_{B}}\Hom_{A}(1_{F}B1_{Y},?):A{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow B{\operatorname{-Mod}}.

We call this
coinduction along
F
.
Since it is right adjoint to an exact functor,
\coind_{F}
is left
exact and takes injectives to injectives.
The functors
\ind_{F}
and
\coind_{F}
are also called
left and right Kan extensions and may be denoted
F_{!}
and
F_{*}
, respectively;
e.g., see
[
SS1
, (2.1.4)]
,
[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
3.6]
.
There are also analogs of
\ind_{F}
and
\coind_{F}
with
left modules replaced by right modules, which we denote by
{{}_{F}\!}\ind
and

{{}_{F}\!}\coind
; in
[
SS2
]
, these are denoted
(F^{\operatorname{op}})_{!}
and
(F^{\operatorname{op}})_{*}
.

Lemma 2.1
.

Let
F:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{B}
be a
\Bbbk
-linear functor as above.

(1)

If
B1_{F}
is a projective right
A
-module then
\ind_{F}
and
{{}_{F}\!}\coind
are exact functors.

(2)

If
1_{F}B
is a projective left
A
-module then
{{}_{F}\!}\ind
and
\coind_{F}
are exact functors.

Proof.

This is obvious from the definitions of these functors.
∎

Suppose that
F,G:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{B}
are
\Bbbk
-linear functors.
A natural transformation
\alpha:F\Rightarrow G

induces natural
transformations
\res_{\alpha}:\res_{F}\Rightarrow\res_{G}
,

\ind_{\alpha}:\ind_{G}\Rightarrow\ind_{F}
and

\coind_{\alpha}:\coind_{G}\Rightarrow\coind_{F}
.
We leave the detailed definitions of these to the reader, just noting that

\ind_{\alpha}
and
\coind_{\alpha}
are the left and right mates of
\res_{\alpha}
.
Similarly,
\alpha
induces natural transformations

{{}_{\alpha}\!}\res:{{}_{G}\!}\res\Rightarrow{{}_{F}\!}\res
,

{{}_{\alpha}\!}\ind:{{}_{F}\!}\ind\Rightarrow{{}_{G}\!}\ind
and
{{}_{\alpha}\!}\coind:{{}_{F}\!}\coind\Rightarrow{{}_{G}\!}\coind
.
Assuming for simplicity
1
1

1

To formulate analogs of

eqs.

2.8
and
2.9
without this assumption, one needs to
work in the strict
2
-category of
\Bbbk
-linear categories.

that
\mathpzc{A}=\mathpzc{B}
, so that
F
and
G
are
\Bbbk
-linear endofunctors of
\mathpzc{A}
, these constructions define
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functors

(2.8)

\displaystyle\res_{*}

\displaystyle:\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(A{\operatorname{-Mod}})^{{\operatorname{rev}}},

\displaystyle\ind_{*},\coind_{*}

\displaystyle:\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})^{{\operatorname{op}}}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(A{\operatorname{-Mod}}),

(2.9)

\displaystyle{{}_{*}\!}\res

\displaystyle:\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})^{{\operatorname{op}}}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}({\operatorname{Mod-}}A)^{{\operatorname{rev}}},

\displaystyle{{}_{*}\!}\ind,{{}_{*}\!}\coind

\displaystyle:\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}({\operatorname{Mod-}}A).

Here,
\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})
denotes the strict monoidal
\Bbbk
-linear
category of
\Bbbk
-linear endofunctors and natural transformations,
“op” means the opposite category with the same monoidal product,
and “rev” means the same category with the reversed monoidal product.

2.3.
Duality

Continue with
A
and
B
be the path algebras of
\mathpzc{A}
and
\mathpzc{B}
, respectively.
There is a contravariant functor

(2.10)

?^{\circledast}:A{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow{\operatorname{Mod-}}A

taking
V=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}V
to
V^{\circledast}:=\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}(1_{X}V)^{*}
, the direct sum of the linear
duals of the “weight spaces”
1_{X}V
.
The restriction of this to locally finite-dimensional modules is an
equivalence, with quasi-inverse given by the restriction of the
analogously-defined duality functor

(2.11)

{{}^{\circledast}}?:{\operatorname{Mod-}}A\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod}}

in the other direction.
To obtain a duality (
=
contravariant auto-equivalence) on

A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
from
eqs.

2.10
and
2.11
, one also needs a
\Bbbk
-linear equivalence
\sigma:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{A}^{\operatorname{op}}
. Restriction along
\sigma
gives equivalences

\res_{\sigma}:{\operatorname{Mod_{lfd}-}}A\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
and

{{}_{\sigma}\!}\res:A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}\rightarrow{\operatorname{Mod_{lfd}-}}A
,
hence, we obtain the
duality functor

(2.12)

?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}:=\res_{\sigma}\circ?^{\circledast}={{}^{\circledast}}?\circ{{}_{\sigma}\!}\res:A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}.

Given a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
F:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{B}
, we obviously
have that

(2.13)

\displaystyle?^{\circledast}\circ\res_{F}

\displaystyle\cong{{}_{F}\!}\res\circ?^{\circledast}

as functors from
B{\operatorname{-Mod}}
to
{\operatorname{Mod-}}A
.
We deduce that

(2.14)

\displaystyle{{}^{\circledast}}?\circ{{}_{F}\!}\ind

\displaystyle\cong\coind_{F}\circ{{}^{\circledast}}?,

\displaystyle{{}^{\circledast}}?\circ{{}_{F}\!}\coind

\displaystyle\cong\ind_{F}\circ{{}^{\circledast}}?

as functors from
{\operatorname{Mod-}}A
to
B{\operatorname{-Mod}}
.

2.4.
Induction product

The
\Bbbk
-linear categories of interest later on will usually
have some additional monoidal structure. In fact, they will be strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal categories defined by generators and relations.
We use the symbol
\star
for the monoidal product in such categories, reserving
\otimes
for the tensor product
\otimes_{\Bbbk}
of vector spaces over
\Bbbk
.
We adopt the usual string calculus for morphisms in strict monoidal
categories, our convention being that
f\circ g
, the composition of

f
and
g
, is drawn as
f
on top of
g
and
f\star g
, the monoidal
product of
f
and
g
, is drawn as
f
to the left of
g
.

Let
\mathpzc{C}
be a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category with
path algebra
C=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{C}}1_{Y}C1_{X}
.
The monoidal product
\star
on
\mathpzc{C}
extends canonically
to
\Kar(\mathpzc{C})
. There is also a monoidal product
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}

making
C{\operatorname{-Proj}}
into a (no longer strict)
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category such that the
contravariant Yoneda equivalence from
\Kar(\mathpzc{C})
to
C{\operatorname{-Proj}}
is
monoidal. This functor
is the restriction of a tensor product functor

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
on the Abelian category
C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
.
We call this the
induction product
.
Category theorists refer to this instead
as
Day convolution
and define it via the coend expression:

V_{1}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}V_{2}=\int^{X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathpzc{C}}\Hom_{\mathpzc{C}}(X_{1}\star X_{2},?)\otimes V_{1}(X_{1})\otimes V_{2}(X_{2}).

We give the algebraist’s formulation of the definition
in the next paragraph; see also
[
SS1
, (2.1.14)]
,
[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
3.10]
.
Using
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
, we can make the split Grothendieck group
K_{0}(C)
into
a ring with
multiplication

(2.15)

[P][Q]:=[P{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}Q].

Its identity element is the isomorphism class of
the distinguished projective module
C1_{\mathbbm{1}}
, where
\mathbbm{1}\in\mathbb{O}_{C}
is
the unit object.

Here is the detailed definition of
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
. Let
\mathpzc{C}\boxtimes\mathpzc{C}
be the
\Bbbk
-linearization of the Cartesian product

\mathpzc{C}\times\mathpzc{C}
. The objects in
\mathpzc{C}\boxtimes\mathpzc{C}
are pairs
(X_{1},X_{2})\in\mathbb{O}_{C}\times\mathbb{O}_{C}
, and the morphism space from
(X_{1},X_{2})
to
(Y_{1},Y_{2})

is
\Hom{C}(X_{1},Y_{1})\otimes\Hom_{\mathpzc{C}}(X_{2},Y_{2})
.
We denote its path algebra by

C\boxtimes C=\bigoplus_{X_{1},X_{2},Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\mathbb{O}_{C}}1_{Y_{1}}C1_{X_{1}}\otimes 1_{Y_{2}}C1_{X_{2}}.

Multiplication in
C\boxtimes C
is the obvious “tensor-wise” product just like for a tensor product of algebras.
If
C
is locally finite-dimensional, so too is
C\boxtimes C
.
Given
V_{1},V_{2}\in C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
, let

V_{1}\boxtimes V_{2}=\bigoplus_{X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{O}_{C}}1_{X_{1}}V_{1}\otimes 1_{X_{2}}V_{2}

be their tensor product over
\Bbbk

viewed as a left
C\boxtimes C
-module in the obvious way.
In fact, this defines a functor

\boxtimes:C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\boxtimes C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow C\boxtimes C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
.
The monoidal product on
\mathpzc{C}
is a
\Bbbk
-linear functor

\star:\mathpzc{C}\boxtimes\mathpzc{C}\rightarrow\mathpzc{C}
.
Let

C1_{\star}=\bigoplus_{X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{O}_{C}}C1_{X_{1}\star X_{2}}

be the
(C,C\boxtimes C)
-bimodule obtained by restricting the right
C
-module
C

along this functor.
Induction along
\star
, that is, the
functor
\ind_{\star}=C1_{\star}\otimes_{C\boxtimes C}:C\boxtimes C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
from
eq.

2.5
, is left adjoint to the
restriction functor
\res_{\star}
from
eq.

2.1
.
Then the induction product is the composition

(2.16)

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}:=\ind_{\star}\circ\;\boxtimes:C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\boxtimes C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow C{\operatorname{-Mod}}.

Thus, for
V_{1},V_{2}\in C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
, we have that

V_{1}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}V_{2}=C1_{\star}\otimes_{C\boxtimes C}(V_{1}\boxtimes V_{2})
.
Associativity of
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}

(up to natural isomorphism) follows from “transitivity of induction”,
i.e., the associativity of tensor products of modules over locally
unital algebras.
We obviously have that

(2.17)

C1_{X_{1}}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}C1_{X_{2}}\cong C1_{X_{1}\star X_{2}}

for
X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{O}_{C}
.
This justifies our earlier assertion that
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
extends the monoidal
product
\star
on

\Kar(\mathpzc{C})
. It also follows that
V_{1}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}V_{2}
is finitely generated if
both
V_{1}
and
V_{2}
are finitely generated.

The induction product
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
is right exact in both arguments,
but in general it is not left exact.
We denote the
i
th left derived functor of
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
on
C
-modules

V,W
by
\Tor_{i}^{C}(V,W)
. This can be computed from a projective
resolution of either
V
or
W
.

Lemma 2.2
.

If
C1_{\star}
is a projective right
C\boxtimes C
-module then
the induction product
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
is biexact.

Proof.

This follows from
lemma

2.1
.
∎

Finally suppose that
\mathpzc{C}
is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear
symmetric
monoidal category, so that there is given a symmetric braiding
R:\star\mathrel{{\mathop{\Rightarrow}\limits}}\star^{\operatorname{rev}}
.
From this, we obtain a braiding
\ind_{R}\circ\boxtimes:{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}^{\operatorname{rev}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\Rightarrow}\limits}}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
making
C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
into a
\Bbbk
-linear
symmetric monoidal category too.

Remark 2.3
.

There is a second convolution product
\underline{{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}}
which we call the
coinduction product
. This is defined by
replacing
\ind_{\star}
with
\coind_{\star}
in
eq.

2.16
. It is easy to understand on
injective rather than projective modules. It will not often be used
subsequently, but note that
the induction and coinduction products are interchanged by duality.

2.5.
Projective functors

Suppose that
\mathpzc{C}
is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear
monoidal category and
\mathpzc{A}
is a
\Bbbk
-linear category, denoting their
path algebras by
C
and
A
as usual.
We say that
\mathpzc{A}
is a
strict
\mathpzc{C}
-module category
if there is
a strictly associative and unital
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor

\star:\mathpzc{C}\boxtimes\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{A}
. Equivalently, this is the
data of a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor

\Psi:\mathpzc{C}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\mathpzc{A})
.
For
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{C}}(X,X^{\prime})
, we sometimes denote the
evaluation of the natural transformation

\Psi(f)
on
Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
simply by
f_{Y}:X\star Y\rightarrow X^{\prime}\star Y
.

The definition of the induction product
\star
from
eq.

2.16

extends naturally to this setting, thereby defining a
\Bbbk
-linear functor

(2.18)

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}:=\ind_{\star}\;\circ\;\boxtimes:C{\operatorname{-Mod}}\boxtimes A{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Mod}}

which makes
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
into a (no longer strict)
C{\operatorname{-Mod}}
-module category.
For objects
X\in\mathbb{O}_{C}
and
Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
, we have
that

(2.19)

C1_{X}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}A1_{Y}\cong A1_{X\star Y},

i.e.,

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
extends
\star:\mathpzc{C}\boxtimes\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{A}
. Using
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
to define the action as in

eq.

2.15
, the split Grothendieck group
K_{0}(A)
becomes a left
module over the split Grothendieck ring
K_{0}(C)
.

Now fix
X\in\mathbb{O}_{C}
and consider the functor
X\star:\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow\mathpzc{A}
.
There is an adjoint pair of endofunctors

(\ind_{X\star},\res_{X\star})
of
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
defined by
induction and restriction along
X\star
:

(2.20)

\displaystyle\ind_{X\star}:=A1_{X\star}\otimes_{A}\qquad\text{where}\qquad A1_{X\star}:=\bigoplus_{Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}A1_{X\star Y},

(2.21)

\displaystyle\res_{X\star}:=1_{X\star}A\otimes_{A}\qquad\text{where}\qquad 1_{X\star}A:=\bigoplus_{Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X\star Y}A.

The general properties discussed earlier give that
\res_{X\star}
is
exact, and
\ind_{X\star}
is right exact and sends
(finitely generated) projectives to (finitely generated) projectives.
Thus,
\ind_{X\star}
restricts to a well-defined functor

\ind_{X\star}:A{\operatorname{-Proj}}\rightarrow A{\operatorname{-Proj}}
.
Note also that

(2.22)

\ind_{X\star}(A1_{Y})\cong A1_{X\star Y}

for all
Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}
.
One can also interpret
\ind_{X\star}
as a special induction product, thanks to the following lemma.

Lemma 2.4
.

For any
X\in\mathbb{O}_{C}
, we have that
\ind_{X\star}\cong C1_{X}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
.

Proof.

This follows from the chain of isomorphisms

\displaystyle A1_{X\star}\otimes_{A}V

\displaystyle\cong(A1_{\star}\otimes_{C\boxtimes A}(C1_{X}\boxtimes A))\otimes_{A}V

\displaystyle\cong A1_{\star}\otimes_{C\boxtimes A}((C1_{X}\boxtimes A)\otimes_{A}V)

\displaystyle\cong A1_{\star}\otimes_{C\boxtimes A}(C1_{X}\boxtimes V)=C1_{X}{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}V

for
V\in A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
.
∎

Let
X,Y
be objects of
\mathpzc{C}
.
Recall that
Y
is a
left dual
of
X
(equivalently,
X
is a
right dual
of
Y
) if there are
evaluation and coevaluation morphisms

\operatorname{ev}:Y\star X\rightarrow\mathbbm{1}
and
\operatorname{coev}:\mathbbm{1}\rightarrow X\star Y

satisfying the zig-zag identities.
In string diagrams, we denote
\operatorname{ev}
and
\operatorname{coev}
by the cap

{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}Y}
{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}

and the cup

{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}
{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}Y}
,
respectively, so that the zig-zag identities become

(2.23)

Corollary 2.6
.

If
X
has a left dual
Y
in
\mathpzc{C}
then
(\ind_{X\star},\ind_{Y\star})
and
(\res_{X\star},\res_{Y\star})

are adjoint pairs of functors.

From the corollary, we deduce that if
X
is
rigid
, i.e., it has both a left and a right dual, then both of the functors

\ind_{X\star}
and
\res_{X\star}
have both a right and a left adjoint.
Moreover, as discussed earlier, both of these functors are exact and
they preserve finitely generated projectives.
We will refer to finite direct sums of direct summands of
endofunctors of
A{\operatorname{-Mod}}
of this sort as
projective functors
.

2.6.
The symmetric category

For a basic example,
we have the
symmetric category

\mathpzc{Sym}
, which is the free strict
\Bbbk
-linear symmetric monoidal category on one object. In string diagrams, we denote this
generating
object simply by
\boldsymbol{|}
; then an arbitrary object is the monoidal
product
\boldsymbol{|}^{\star n}
for some
n\geq 0
.
Morphisms in
\mathpzc{Sym}
are generated by
a single morphism depicted by the crossing

(2.25)

Sometimes it is convenient to identify objects in
\mathpzc{Sym}
with natural numbers, so that the object set
\{\boldsymbol{|}^{\star n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}

of
\mathpzc{Sym}
is identified with
\mathbb{N}
.
For
m,n\geq 0
, the morphism space
\Hom{Sym}(n,m)

is
\{0\}
if
m\neq n
, while if
m=n
it consists of
\Bbbk
-linear
combinations of string diagrams representing permutations in the
symmetric group
S_{n}
, i.e., we have that
\End_{\mathpzc{Sym}}(n)=\Bbbk S_{n}.

Note our general convention here is to number strings by

Let
{S\!ym}
be the path algebra of
\mathpzc{Sym}
.
Thus, we have that

(2.27)

{S\!ym}=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\Bbbk S_{n}.

Since
\Bbbk
is of characteristic zero, we deduce from Maschke’s theorem that

{S\!ym}
is a
semisimple
locally unital algebra.
In this case, the induction product
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
making
{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod}}
into a monoidal category
is nothing more than
the usual induction product
on representations of the symmetric groups:
we have that

V{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}W=\ind_{S_{n}\times S_{m}}^{S_{n+m}}(V\boxtimes W)

for
V\in\Bbbk S_{n}{\operatorname{-Mod}}
and
W\in\Bbbk S_{m}{\operatorname{-Mod}}
.
In fact, the induction product
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
and the
coinduction product
\underline{{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}}
on
{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod}}
are isomorphic as
\ind_{S_{n}\times S_{m}}^{S_{n+m}}\cong\coind_{S_{n}\times S_{m}}^{S_{n+m}}
(as
always for finite groups).

Recall that the irreducible
\Bbbk S_{n}
-modules are the

Specht modules

S(\lambda)
parametrized by the set
\mathcal{P}_{n}

of partitions
\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots)
of
n
.
Hence, the irreducible
{S\!ym}
-modules are
the Specht modules
S(\lambda)
parametrized by all partitions

\lambda\in\mathcal{P}=\bigsqcup_{n\geq 0}\mathcal{P}_{n}
.
We sometimes write
|\lambda|
for the size
\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\cdots
of
a partition
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
, and
\ell(\lambda)
for its length, that is, the number of non-zero parts.
We will often identify
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
with its Young diagram.
For example, the partition
(5,3^{2},2)
is identified with

The Grothendieck ring
K_{0}({S\!ym})
of the symmetric category is positively graded
with degree
n
component being
K_{0}(\Bbbk S_{n})
. It is well known that

K_{0}({S\!ym})
is canonically isomorphic as a graded ring
to the
ring of symmetric functions

\Lambda=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\Lambda_{n}
,
with the class
[S(\lambda)]
of the Specht module corresponding under the isomorphism to the

Schur function

s_{\lambda}\in\Lambda
.
In
\Lambda
, we have that

(2.28)

s_{\mu}s_{\nu}=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}}LR_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_{\lambda}

where

LR_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}
is the Littlewood-Richardson coefficient.
Since
{S\!ym}
is semisimple, this is equivalent to the existence of an isomorphism

(2.29)

S(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S(\nu)\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}}S(\lambda)^{\oplus LR_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}}

at the level of modules.
Later on, we will also need the “triple” Littlewood-Richardson coefficient

(2.30)

\displaystyle LR^{\kappa}_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}

\displaystyle:=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}LR^{\gamma}_{\lambda,\mu}LR^{\kappa}_{\gamma,\nu}=[S(\lambda){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S(\nu):S(\kappa)].

The
content
of the node in row
i
and column
j
of a Young diagram is the integer
c=j-i
. Let
\operatorname{add}(\lambda)
be the set consisting of the
contents of the
addable nodes

of
\lambda
, that is, the places in the Young diagram where a node can be added to
the diagram to obtain a new Young diagram.
Similarly, let
\operatorname{rem}(\lambda)
be the set of contents of the
removable nodes

of
\lambda
, that is, the places in the Young diagram where a node can be removed from the diagram to obtain a new Young diagram.
Note that all of the addable and removable nodes of a Young diagram
are of different contents (another of the benefits of working in
characteristic zero).
For
a\in\operatorname{add}(\lambda)
, let
\lambda+\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle a}\>\,
be the partition obtained by adding
the unique addable node of content
a
to the diagram.
For
b\in\operatorname{rem}(\lambda)
, let
\lambda-\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle b}\>\,
be the partition obtained by removing the unique removable node of content
b
from the diagram.

The combinatorial notions just introduced arise naturally on
considering
branching rules
for the symmetric group. In our
setup, the sums over all
n\geq 0
of the usual
restriction and
induction functors

\res_{S_{n}}^{S_{n+1}}
and

\ind_{S_{n}}^{S_{n+1}}=\Bbbk S_{n+1}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{n}}

are isomorphic to the functors

(2.31)

\displaystyle F

\displaystyle:=\res_{\boldsymbol{|}\,\star}:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}},

\displaystyle E

\displaystyle:=\ind_{\boldsymbol{|}\,\star}:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}},

notation as in
eqs.

2.20
and
2.21
.
This follows because
the functor

The effect of the functors

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{a\in\operatorname{add}(\lambda)}S(\lambda+\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle a}\>\,).

3.
The partition category and its triangular decomposition

Next we introduce the partition category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
, which we define by
generators and relations. We then
make some basic observations about its representation theory.
Most of the results here are due to Sam and Snowden
[
SS2
, Sec. 6]
, but we
have tried to give a self-contained account since our general notation and other
conventions are often different. The most important point is
that the path algebra
Par_{t}
of the category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

has a triangular decomposition, hence, the category of locally finite-dimensional

Par_{t}
-modules is an upper finite highest weight category in the
sense of
[
BS
,
\lx@sectionsign
3.3]
.
In fact,
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is a monoidal triangular category in the sense of
Sam and Snowden.

3.1.
The partition category

t\in\Bbbk
be a parameter. According to the following definition,
the partition category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is the free strict
\Bbbk
-linear
symmetric monoidal category generated by a commutative Frobenius object which is special of categorical dimension
t
.

The object set of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is
\{\boldsymbol{|}^{\star n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}
. We will sometimes denote

\boldsymbol{|}^{\star n}
simply by
n
, so that the object set is identified with
\mathbb{N}
.

The relations
eqs.

3.2
and
3.3
imply that
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is a

symmetric
monoidal category,
eqs.

3.4
and
3.5
imply that the generating object is a
commutative Frobenius object
, and the first relation from

eq.

3.6
means that this object is actually a
special

Frobenius object.
The symmetric monoidal category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is
rigid
with every object being self-dual.
To justify this,
it is enough to specify the evaluation and coevaluation morphisms

\operatorname{ev}:\boldsymbol{|}\star\boldsymbol{|}\to\mathbbm{1}
and
\operatorname{coev}:\mathbbm{1}\to\boldsymbol{|}\star\boldsymbol{|}

for the generating object, which we represent graphically by
the cap and cup:

These satisfy the zig-zag identities as in
eq.

2.23
, as may easily be checked using

eq.

3.5
.
Now the relations in
eq.

3.6
imply that the

categorical dimension
of the generating object is
t
.

By an
m\times n
partition diagram
, we mean a
string diagram
f

representing a morphism in
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)

obtained by horizontally and vertically composing the generating morphisms
eq.

3.1
,
such that every connected component of
f
has at least one endpoint, i.e., is not a “floating bubble”. In view of
the dimension relation in
eq.

3.6
,
floating bubbles can be contracted then removed,
multiplying the result by the scalar
t
each time this occurs. It follows that
every morphism in
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)

can be written as a
\Bbbk
-linear combination of
m\times n
partition diagrams.
Let
\sigma:\mathpzc{Par}_{t}\rightarrow(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})^{\operatorname{op}}

be the strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor that is the identity on
objects and sends the generating morphisms to their flips in a
horizontal axis. More generally,
\sigma
sends an

m\times n
partition diagram to the
n\times m
partition diagram that is its flip in a horizontal axis.

The above definition of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
by generators and relations
is not the most common definition found in the literature.
It was first formulated in this way
by Comes in
[
C
, Th. 2.1]
; see also
[
LSR
, Prop. 2.1]
.
In the more traditional approach (e.g., see
[
D
,
\lx@sectionsign
8]
and
[
CO
, Def. 2.11]
), one instead defines
the morphism space
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)
to be the vector space with basis labelled by set partitions of

\{1,\dots,n,1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}
, giving explicit combinatorial rules for the horizontal and vertical compositions in terms of these partitions.
Suppose that
f
is an
m\times n
partition diagram.
Labelling the endpoints of
f
from right to left by
1,\dots,n
on the bottom bounadry and
1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}
on the top boundary as in the following example, the diagram
f

determines a partition of the set

\{1,\dots,n,1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}

with parts
arising from the labels at the endpoints of the connected components in the diagram.
For example, the
9\times 7
partition diagram

(3.8)

{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}7}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}6}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}5}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}4}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}9^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}8^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}7^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}6^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}5^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}4^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1^{\prime}}

determines the partition

\{1,4,1^{\prime},2^{\prime},3^{\prime},4^{\prime},6^{\prime},8^{\prime}\}\sqcup\{2,6\}\sqcup\{3,5,9^{\prime}\}\sqcup\{7,5^{\prime}\}\sqcup\{7^{\prime}\}.

In this way, one obtains a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor
from the category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
defined by generators and relations as above to the
category
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
as defined via the more traditional combinatorial approach.
Then the result of Comes just mentioned asserts that this functor is an
isomorphism.

The discussion in the previous paragraph shows that
two
m\times n
partition diagrams represent the same morphism
in
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)

if and only if the diagrams are equivalent in the sense that they
determine the same partition of the set

\{1,\dots,n,1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}
labelling their endpoints.
For example, the morphism represented by
eq.

3.8
is equal to the
one represented by the tidier diagram

(3.9)

{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}7}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}6}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}5}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}4}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}9^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}8^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}7^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}6^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}5^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}4^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2^{\prime}}
{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1^{\prime}}

because this determines the same partition of the set labelling the endpoints.
In fact, Comes’ result implies that
any set of representatives for the equivalence classes

m\times n
partition diagrams
give a
basis
for the morphism space
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)
.
In particular,

\dim\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)
is equal to the
the
(m+n)
th
Bell number
which counts set partitions of
m+n
.
Taking
m=n=0
, this implies that

(3.10)

\End_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(\mathbbm{1})=\Bbbk.

We say that
c
is a
double tree
if
c
has more than one endpoint at the top and more than one endpoint at the bottom. In that case, it is equivalent to the composition of an upward tree and a downward tree; for example, the rightmost connected component in
eq.

3.9
is a double tree.
Finally we say that
c
is a
trunk
if
c
has exactly one endpoint both at the top and at the bottom:

c=\>\hbox to0.8pt{\vbox to23.56pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.4pt\lower-0.4pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

Any connected component of a partition diagram can be represented
either as an upward branch, an upward leaf, an upward tree,
a downward branch, a downward leaf, a downward tree, a double tree, or a trunk.

Let
f
be an
m\times n
partition diagram. We say
f
is

•

a
permutation diagram

if all of its connected components are trunks, in which case we must have that
m=n
;

•

an
upward partition diagram

if its connected components are trunks, upward branches, upward leaves and upward trees, in which case we must have that
m\geq n
;

•

a
downward partition diagram
if its connected components are trunks, downward branches, downward leaves and downward trees, in which case we must have that
m\leq n
.

Let
f
be an upward
m\times n
partition diagram. We say that it is

strictly upward
if
m>n
.
Let
c_{1},\dots,c_{k}
be the connected components of
f
that are either trunks or upward trees, indexing them
so that their bottom endpoints are in order from right to left in
f
.
We say that
f
is
normally ordered
if the rightmost of the top endpoints of each of
c_{1},\dots,c_{k}
are also in order from right to left in
f
.
In other words,
f
is normally ordered if it can be drawn so that the right edges of all of the upward trees and trunks in
f
are non-crossing.
Similarly, we define
strictly downward
and

normally ordered
downward partition diagrams.

Now we can define some monoidal subcategories of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
.
Let
\mathpzc{Sym}
be the symmetric category as defined in
section

2.6
.
There is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear symmetric monoidal functor

(3.11)

i_{t}^{\circ}:\mathpzc{Sym}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

sending the generating object and the generating morphism of
\mathpzc{Sym}

to the
generating object and the generating morphism of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
that is represented by the crossing. Using the basis theorem for morphism spaces
in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
, it follows that this functor
is faithful. We use it to
identify

\mathpzc{Sym}
with a monoidal
subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. In other words,
\mathpzc{Sym}
is
identified with the subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
consisting of all objects
and all the morphisms which can be written as linear combinations of permutation diagrams.

Next, let
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
be the strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category generated by one object
\boldsymbol{|}
and the morphisms

(3.12)

\displaystyle:\boldsymbol{|}\star\boldsymbol{|}\to\boldsymbol{|}\star\boldsymbol{|}\ ,

\displaystyle:\boldsymbol{|}\to\boldsymbol{|}\star\boldsymbol{|}\ ,

{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ

\displaystyle:\mathbbm{1}\to\boldsymbol{|}

subject to the relations
eqs.

3.2
,
3.3
and
3.4
and their
flips in a vertical axis.
We call this the
upward partition category
.
The cup can also be defined in
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
as in
eq.

3.7
.
Any upward partition diagram can be interpreted as a string diagram representing a morphism in
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
.
Moreover, the defining relations in
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
imply that
two upward
m\times n
partition diagrams which are equivalent in the sense that
they define the same partition of the set

\{1,\dots,n,1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}
labelling the
endpoints
are also equal as morphisms in

\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}}(n,m)
.
There is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor

(3.13)

i_{t}^{\flat}:\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

sending the generating morphisms of
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}

to the corresponding ones in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. As equivalence classes of upward
m\times n
partition diagrams span
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}}(n,m)

and their images in
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)
are linearly independent, this functor is faithful.
We use it to
identify

\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
with a monoidal
subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. In other words,
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
is
identified with the monoidal subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
consisting of all objects
and all of the morphisms which can be written as linear combinations of upward partition diagrams.
Also let
\mathpzc{Par}^{-}
be the monoidal subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
consisting of all objects and all of the
morphisms which can be written as linear combinations of normally ordered upward partition diagrams.

Similarly to the previous paragraph, we define
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
, the
downward partition category
, to be the strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category generated by one object
\boldsymbol{|}
and the morphisms that are the flips
of
eq.

3.12
in a horizontal axis, subject to the relations that are the flips of the ones for
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}
. The cap can also be defined in
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
as in
eq.

3.7
.
Evidently,
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}\cong(\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat})^{\operatorname{op}}
with isomorphism being defined by the flip
\sigma
in a horizontal axis.
There is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor

(3.14)

i_{t}^{\sharp}:\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

sending the generating morphisms of
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}

to the corresponding ones in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
.
We have that
i_{t}^{\sharp}=\sigma\circ i_{t}^{\flat}\circ\sigma
, so we
deduce from the previous paragraph that
i_{t}^{\sharp}
is faithful too.
We use it to
identify

\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
with a monoidal
subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. In other words,
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
is
identified with the monoidal subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
consisting of all objects
and all of the morphisms which can be written as linear combinations of downward partition diagrams.
Also let
\mathpzc{Par}^{+}
be the monoidal subcategory of
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
consisting of all objects and all of the morphisms which can be written as linear combinations of normally ordered downward partition diagrams.

Finally we let
Par_{t}
be the path algebra of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
. It is a locally unital algebra
with distinguished idempotents
\{1_{n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}
arising from the identity endomorphisms of the objects of
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
.
We also have the path algebras

Par^{\flat},Par^{-},{S\!ym},Par^{+},Par^{\sharp}

of
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat},\mathpzc{Par}^{-},\mathpzc{Sym},\mathpzc{Par}^{+},\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
, which we may view as
locally unital subalgebras of
Par_{t}
via the embeddings

eqs.

3.11
,
3.13
and
3.14
. The following theorem is
the
triangular decomposition
of
Par_{t}
.

Theorem 3.2
.

Let
\mathbb{K}:=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\Bbbk 1_{n}
viewed as a
locally unital subalgebra of
Par_{t}
. Multiplication defines a linear isomorphism

(3.15)

\displaystyle Par^{-}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}{S\!ym}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}Par^{+}

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Par_{t}.

Hence, we also have isomorphisms

(3.16)

\displaystyle Par^{-}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}{S\!ym}

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Par^{\flat},

(3.17)

\displaystyle{S\!ym}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}Par^{+}

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Par^{\sharp},

(3.18)

\displaystyle Par^{\flat}\otimes_{{S\!ym}}Par^{\sharp}

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Par_{t}.

Proof.

Any partition diagram is equivalent to a diagram
that is the composition of a normally ordered upward partition diagram, a permutation diagram, and a normally ordered downward partition diagram; see
eq.

3.9
for an example of such a decomposition.
Moreover, equivalence classes of these sorts of
diagrams give bases for
Par_{t}
,
Par^{-},{S\!ym}
and
Par^{+}
. This
implies that
eq.

3.15
is an isomorphism.
Then
eqs.

3.16
,
3.17
and
3.18
follow as in
[
BS
, Rem. 5.32]
.
∎

theorem

3.2
is all that is needed to see that
the locally finite-dimensional locally unital algebra

Par_{t}=\bigoplus_{m,n\in\mathbb{N}}1_{m}Par_{t}1_{n}

has a
split triangular
decomposition
in the sense of
[
BS
, Rem. 5.32]
.
Its negative and positive Borel subalgebras are
Par^{\flat}
and
Par^{\sharp}
,
and its Cartan subalgebra is
{S\!ym}=Par^{\flat}\cap Par^{\sharp}
.
The set
I
in the notation of
[
BS
]
is the set
\mathbb{N}

indexing the distinguished idempotents
\{1_{n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}
. The upper finite
poset
(\Lambda,\leq)
in the setup of
[
BS
]
is
(\mathbb{N},\geq)
; we stress
that the ordering is reversed here, as it has to be in order to have an upper finite poset, thereby conforming to the general conventions of
[
BS
]
.
The function
\partial
from
[
BS
]
is the identity function.

As
{S\!ym}
is semisimple, this discussion
shows equivalently that
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is a triangular category in the
sense of
[
SS2
, Def. 4.1]
. Its upward and downward
subcategories
\mathpzc{U}
and
\mathpzc{D}
in the setup of
loc. cit.
are
\mathpzc{Par}^{\flat}

and
\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}
, respectively. In fact,
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is a
monoidal
triangular category
as defined in
[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
4.11]
, as was
established already by Sam and Snowden in
[
SS2
, Prop. 6.3]
.
This means that induction commutes with induction product: we have that

(3.19)

\displaystyle\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par_{t}}(V{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}W)

\displaystyle\cong(\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par_{t}}V){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}(\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par_{t}}W),

for

{S\!ym}
-modules
V
and
W
. This is
easily seen directly from the definition of the induction product
using

i_{t}^{\circ}\circ\star\cong\star\circ(i_{t}^{\circ}\boxtimes i_{t}^{\circ})
. Similarly,

(3.20)

\displaystyle\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}(V{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}W)

\displaystyle\cong(\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}V){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}(\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}W),

\displaystyle\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}(V{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}W)

\displaystyle\cong(\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}V){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}(\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}W).

3.3.
Classification of irreducible modules and highest weight structure

As
Par_{t}
has a triangular decomposition with Cartan subalgebra
{S\!ym}
being semisimple, we can appeal to the general results of

[
BS
,
\lx@sectionsign
5.5]
to obtain the classification of irreducible

Par_{t}
-modules. Alternatively, this follows from the results in

[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
5.5]
, but note that Sam and Snowden use the language of
lowest weight

rather than
highest weight
categories.
Since isomorphism classes of irreducible
Par_{t}
-modules are in bijection with isomorphism classes of indecomposable projective
Par_{t}
-modules, and the latter are identified with isomorphism classes of indecomposable objects in

\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})
, the results discussed
in this subsection are equivalent to the classification obtained originally in
[
CO
, Th. 3.7]
.

The algebra
Par_{t}
is
\mathbb{Z}
-graded with
1_{m}Par_{t}1_{n}
being in
degree
m-n
. The induced gradings on the
subalgebras
Par^{\flat}
and
Par^{\sharp}
make these into positively
and negatively graded algebras, respectively, with degree zero
components in both cases being the semisimple algebra
{S\!ym}
.
It follows that
the Jacobson radicals of

Par^{\flat}
and
Par^{\sharp}
are the direct sums of their non-zero graded
components. Moreover, the quotients by their Jacobson radicals are
naturally identified with
{S\!ym}
, i.e., there are
locally
unital algebra homomorphisms

(3.21)

\displaystyle\pi^{\flat}:

\displaystyle Par^{\flat}\twoheadrightarrow{S\!ym},

\displaystyle\pi^{\sharp}:

\displaystyle Par^{\sharp}\twoheadrightarrow{S\!ym}.

Let

\infl^{\sharp}:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
and
\infl^{\flat}:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow Par^{\flat}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}

be the functors defined by restriction along these
homomorphisms.
The modules

(3.22)

\displaystyle\big\{S^{\flat}(\lambda):=\infl^{\flat}S(\lambda)\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\},

\displaystyle\big\{S^{\sharp}(\lambda):=\infl^{\sharp}S(\lambda)\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}

give full sets of pairwise inequivalent irreducible modules for

Par^{\flat}
and
Par^{\sharp}
, respectively.

As in
[
BS
, (5.13)–(5.14)]
, we define the
standardization
and
costandardization functors

(3.23)

\displaystyle j_{!}:=\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}\circ\infl^{\sharp}

\displaystyle:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}},

(3.24)

\displaystyle j_{*}:=\coind_{Par^{\flat}}^{Par_{t}}\circ\infl^{\flat}

\displaystyle:{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}},

where
\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}:=Par_{t}\otimes_{Par^{\sharp}}
and

\coind_{Par^{\flat}}^{Par_{t}}:=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\Hom_{Par^{\flat}}(Par_{t}1_{n},?)
. From
eqs.

3.15
,
3.16
and
3.17
it follows that
Par_{t}
is projective both as a right

Par^{\sharp}
-module and as a left
Par^{\flat}
-module, hence, these
functors are exact. Then we define the
standard

and
costandard modules
for
Par_{t}
by

(3.25)

\displaystyle\Delta(\lambda)

\displaystyle:=j_{!}S(\lambda)=\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}S^{\sharp}(\lambda),

\displaystyle\nabla(\lambda)

\displaystyle=j_{*}S(\lambda)=\ind_{Par^{\flat}}^{Par_{t}}S^{\flat}(\lambda),

respectively.

Theorem 3.3
.

The
Par_{t}
-modules
\{L(\lambda)\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\}
defined from

L(\lambda):=\operatorname{hd}\Delta(\lambda)\cong\operatorname{soc}\nabla(\lambda)

give a complete set of pairwise inequivalent irreducible left
Par_{t}
-modules.
Moreover,
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
is an upper finite highest weight category
in the sense of
[
BS
, Def. 3.34]

with weight poset
(\mathcal{P},\preceq)
, where
\preceq
is the partial order on
\mathcal{P}

defined by
\lambda\preceq\mu
if and only if either
\lambda=\mu
or

|\lambda|>|\mu|
. Its standard and costandard objects are the
modules
\Delta(\lambda)
and
\nabla(\lambda)
, respectively.

Proof.

This follows immediately from
[
BS
, Cor. 5.39]
using the triangular decomposition from

theorem

3.2
and the semisimplicity of
{S\!ym}
;
see also
[
SS2
,
\lx@sectionsign
5.5]
.
∎

The fact established in
theorem

3.3
that
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
is an upper finite highest weight category has several significant consequences.
As for any Schurian category,
L(\lambda)
has a projective cover we denote by
P(\lambda)\in Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
.
Let
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
be the exact subcategory of
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
consisting of all modules with a
\Delta
-flag, that is, a finite filtration whose sections are
of the form
\Delta(\lambda)
for
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
.
For any

V\in Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
, the multiplicity
(V:\Delta(\mu))
of
\Delta(\mu)
as a section of some
\Delta
-flag in
V
is well-defined independent of the flag, indeed, it can be calculated from

(3.26)

(V:\Delta(\mu))=\dim\Hom_{Par_{t}}(V,\nabla(\mu)).

This follows from the fundamental
\Ext
-vanishing property
of highest weight categories, namely, that

(3.27)

\dim\Ext^{i}_{Par_{t}}(\Delta(\lambda),\nabla(\mu))=\delta_{i,0}\delta_{\lambda,\mu}

for any
\lambda,\mu\in\mathcal{P}
and
i\geq 0
; see
[
BS
, Lem. 3.48]
.
The definition of highest weight category gives that
P(\lambda)
has a
\Delta
-flag,
so that
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Proj}}
is a full subcategory of
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
.
Moreover, from
eq.

3.26
, one obtains the usual
BGG reciprocity formula

(3.28)

(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\nabla(\mu):L(\lambda)].

The functor
\sigma:\mathpzc{Par}_{t}\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})^{\operatorname{op}}
defined by flipping diagrams in a horizontal axis
can also be viewed as a locally unital anti-involution of the
algebra
Par_{t}
. It interchanges the subalgebras
Par^{\flat}
and
Par^{\sharp}
, and restricts
to an anti-involution also denoted
\sigma
on the subalgebra
{S\!ym}
.
Let
?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}
be the duality on
{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
taking a finite-dimensional
left
{S\!ym}
-module to its linear dual viewed again as a left module using the anti-automorphism
\sigma
.
Since
\sigma(g)=g^{-1}
for a permutation
g\in S_{n}\subset{S\!ym}
,
this is the usual duality on each of the subcategories
\Bbbk S_{n}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
.
It is well known that the irreducible
\Bbbk S_{n}
-modules are self-dual,
hence,

(3.29)

S(\lambda)^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\cong S(\lambda)

for all
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
.
There is also a duality
?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}
on
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
defined as in

eq.

2.12
. Similarly, as
\sigma
interchanges
Par^{\flat}
and

Par^{\sharp}
, we get contravariant equivalences also denoted
?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}
between

Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
and
Par^{\flat}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
.
Similarly to
eqs.

2.13
and
2.14
, we have that

(3.30)

\displaystyle?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\circ\infl^{\flat}

\displaystyle\cong\infl^{\sharp}\circ?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt},

\displaystyle\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}\circ?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}

\displaystyle\cong?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\circ\coind_{Par^{\flat}}^{Par_{t}}.

Hence:

(3.31)

\displaystyle j_{!}\circ?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}

\displaystyle\cong?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\circ j_{*},

\displaystyle j_{*}\circ?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}

\displaystyle\cong?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\circ j_{!}

as functors from

{S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
to
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
.
Then from
eqs.

3.29
and
3.31
, we deduce that

(3.32)

\displaystyle\Delta(\lambda)^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}

\displaystyle\cong\nabla(\lambda),

\displaystyle\nabla(\lambda)^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}

\displaystyle\cong\Delta(\lambda),

\displaystyle L(\lambda)^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}\cong L(\lambda)

for
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
.

Remark 3.4
.

In fact, the duality
?^{\scriptscriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-4.83694pt\sigma\hskip 0.28453pt}
is a
Chevalley duality
of
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{lfd}}}
in the sense of
[
BS
, Def. 4.49]
. The general construction from
[
BS
, Cor. 5.36,
Rem. 5.40]
can be used to show that
Par_{t}
admits a basis making
it into an upper finite
symmetrically based quasi-hereditary algebra in the sense of
[
BS
, Def. 5.1]
.
Equivalently,
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
is an object-adapted cellular category in the sense of
[
EL
, Def. 2.1]
.

3.4.
The downward partition category and reduced Kronecker
coefficients

The results in this subsection are the analogs for the downward partition
category of the results proved in

[
SS1
,
\lx@sectionsign\lx@sectionsign
7.5–7.6]
for the downward Brauer and downward
walled Brauer categories.
The methods are similar. In the first lemma, our standing assumption that

\operatorname{char}\Bbbk=0
is essential in
order to define the idempotent
1_{l,m,n}^{d}
.

Lemma 3.5

(cf.
[
SS2
, Prop. 6.5]
)
.

The right
Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes Par^{\sharp}
-module
Par^{\sharp}1_{\star}

is projective. Consequently, by
lemma

2.2
, the induction product

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}:Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod}}\boxtimes Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod}}\rightarrow Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod}}

is biexact. More precisely,
for integers
l,m,n\geq 0
and
0\leq d\leq\min(l+m-n,l+n-m,m+n-l)

\displaystyle:=(l+m-n-d)/2
