so that
there are
a
nested caps at the
bottom,

b
parallel trunks on the right,

c
parallel trunks on the left,
and
d
nested downward binary trees in the middle.
Also let
1_{l,m,n}^{d}

be the image of the idempotent
\frac{1}{a!}\sum_{w\in S_{a}}w

under the embedding
\Bbbk S_{a}\hookrightarrow\Bbbk(S_{m}\times S_{n})<1_{m}Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes 1_{n}Par^{\sharp}

sending
w\in S_{a}
to the diagram representing the permutation
of

m+n,\dots,1+n,n,\dots,1
defined by

1+n-i\mapsto 1+n-w(i)
,
i+n\mapsto w(i)+n
for

i=1,\dots,a
,
and fixing all other points (i.e., it arises from a permutation of the
a

nested caps in the above picture).
Finally, let
S_{l}/S_{c}\times S_{d}\times S_{b}
be a set of coset
representatives viewed as a subset of
{S\!ym}
via the usual embedding
(in particular,
S_{c}
and
S_{b}
are permuting the leftmost
c
and
rightmost
b
strings, respectively).
Then there is a right
Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes Par^{\sharp}
-module isomorphism

\bigoplus_{l,m,n\geq 0}\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}d=0\\
d\equiv l+m+n\;(2)\end{subarray}}^{\min(l+m-n,l+n-m,m+n-l)}\bigoplus_{g\in S_{l}/S_{c}\times S_{d}\times S_{b}}1_{l,m,n}^{d}(Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes Par^{\sharp})\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Par^{\sharp}1_{\star}

taking the idempotent
1_{l,m,n}^{d}
in the
g
-th summand on the left
hand side to
g\circ f^{d}_{l,m,n}
.

Proof.

This follows on considering the bases for
1_{l}Par^{\sharp}

and

1_{m}Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes 1_{n}Par^{\sharp}
given by equivalence
classes of downward partition diagrams.
∎

Recall for
\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
that the
Kronecker
coefficients
are defined to be the structure constants
for the internal Kronecker product on representations of the symmetric group
S_{n}
:

(3.35)

G^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}=[S(\mu)\otimes S(\nu):S(\lambda)]=\dim\left(S(\lambda)\otimes S(\mu)\otimes S(\nu)\right)^{S_{n}}.

Obviously from the second equality,
G^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
is invariant
under permuting the partitions
\lambda,\mu,\nu
.
For a partition
\lambda
and
n\geq|\lambda|+\lambda_{1}
,
let
\lambda(n)
denote
(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots)\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
.
By a classical result of Murnaghan, for
\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}
, the value of the
Kronecker coeffcient
G^{\lambda(n),}_{\mu(n),\nu(n)}
stabilizes
as
n\rightarrow\infty
; see
[
BOR
]
for more background.
The stable value is the
reduced Kronecker coefficient
,
denoted
\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
. Like the Kronecker
coefficients themselves,
\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
is
invariant under permutations of
\lambda,\mu
and
\nu
.

Example 3.6
.

For any
\lambda,\mu\in\mathcal{P}
, the reduced Kronecker coefficient

\overline{G}^{\mu}_{\boxvoid,\lambda}
is equal to zero
unless
\mu=\lambda+\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle a}\>\,
for some
a\in\operatorname{add}(\lambda)
,

\mu=\lambda-\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle b}\>\,
for some
b\in\operatorname{rem}(\lambda)
,
or
\mu=(\lambda-\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle b}\>\,)+\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle a}\>\,
for some
b\in\operatorname{rem}(\lambda)

and
a=\operatorname{add}(\lambda-\,{\displaystyle\boxvoid}\hskip-6.25958pt{\scriptstyle b}\>\,)
.
In these cases,
\overline{G}^{\mu}_{\boxvoid,\lambda}
is
1
if
\mu\neq\lambda
and
|\operatorname{rem}(\lambda)|
if
\mu=\lambda
.
To see this using
the definition just given, consider
the natural
n
-dimensional permutation module for the symmetric group

U_{n}\cong S((n-1,1))\oplus S((n))
and note that
the functor
U_{n}\otimes
is isomorphic to
\ind_{S_{n-1}}^{S_{n}}\circ\res_{S_{n-1}}^{S_{n}}
.

Lemma 3.7
.

Take
l,m,n\geq 0
and

0\leq d\leq\min(l+m-n,l+n-m,m+n-l)
with
d\equiv l+m+n\pmod{2}
, and define
a,b,c

according to
eq.

3.33
. Let
\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}
be the set of partitions of

\{1,\dots,l\}\sqcup\{1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}\sqcup\{1^{\prime\prime},\dots,n^{\prime\prime}\}

such that exactly
a
of the parts are subsets of the form

\{j^{\prime},k^{\prime\prime}\}
, exactly
b
of the parts are subsets of the form

\{i,k^{\prime\prime}\}
, exactly
c
of the parts are subsets of the form

\{i,j^{\prime}\}
, and the remaining
d
parts are subsets of the
form
\{i,j^{\prime},k^{\prime\prime}\}
for
i\in\{1,\dots,l\}
,
j^{\prime}\in\{1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}
and
k^{\prime\prime}\in\{1^{\prime\prime},\dots,n^{\prime\prime}\}
as suggested
by the picture:

\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\scriptstyle\>\>1\,\cdots\>l\>\>
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\scriptstyle\>1^{\prime}\,\cdots\>m^{\prime}\>
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\scriptstyle 1^{\prime\prime}\,\cdots\>n^{\prime\prime}
\scriptstyle a
\scriptstyle c
\scriptstyle b
\scriptstyle d

The group
S_{l}\times S_{m}\times S_{n}
acts on the left on

\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}
so that
S_{l}
permutes
\{1,\dots,l\}
,
S_{m}

permutes

\{1^{\prime},\dots,m^{\prime}\}
and
S_{n}
permutes
\{1^{\prime\prime},\dots,n^{\prime\prime}\}
.
Let
\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}
be the linearization, which is a

\Bbbk(S_{l}\times S_{m}\times S_{n})
-module.
For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{l},\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{m},\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
we
have that

[\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}:S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{P}_{a},\beta\in\mathcal{P}_{b},\gamma\in\mathcal{P}_{c}\\
\delta,\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{d}\end{subarray}}LR^{\lambda}_{\beta,\gamma,\delta}LR^{\mu}_{\alpha,\gamma,\delta^{\prime}}LR^{\nu}_{\alpha,\beta,\delta^{\prime\prime}}G^{\delta}_{\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}}.

Proof.

Let
G:=S_{l}\times S_{m}\times S_{n}
,
P
be the parabolic
subgroup
(S_{b}\times S_{d}\times S_{c})\times(S_{c}\times S_{d}\times S_{a})\times(S_{a}\times S_{d}\times S_{b})\leq G

and
L
be the subgroup
S_{a}\times S_{b}\times S_{c}\times S_{d}\leq P

embedded diagonally via the map

(x,y,z,w)\mapsto(y,w,z;z,w,x;x,w,y).

The action of
G
on
\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}
is transitive and
the subgroup
L
is a point stabilizer. Hence, the
\Bbbk G
-module
\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}

is induced from
\triv_{L}
, the trivial
\Bbbk L
-module. By Frobenius reciprocity, it follows that

[\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}:S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)]=\dim(S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu))^{L}.

The restriction of
S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)
to the parabolic subgroup
P
is isomorphic to

\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\alpha^{\prime},\beta,\beta^{\prime},\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\\
\delta,\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{d}\end{subarray}}\hskip-11.38109pt\Big(\big(S(\beta)\boxtimes S(\delta)\boxtimes S(\gamma^{\prime})\big)\boxtimes\big(S(\gamma)\boxtimes S(\delta^{\prime})\boxtimes S(\alpha^{\prime})\big)\boxtimes\big(S(\alpha)\boxtimes S(\delta^{\prime\prime})\boxtimes S(\beta^{\prime})\big)\Big)^{\oplus N}.

where
N:=LR^{\lambda}_{\beta,\delta,\gamma^{\prime}}LR^{\mu}_{\gamma,\delta^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}}LR^{\nu}_{\alpha,\delta^{\prime\prime\prime},\beta^{\prime}}
.
By Schur’s lemma, this contributes to the
L
-fixed points only from the summands
with
\alpha=\alpha^{\prime},\beta=\beta^{\prime}
and
\gamma=\gamma^{\prime}
, and for
each of those summands the contribution is
G^{\delta}_{\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}}
by
eq.

3.35
.
∎

Since
Par^{\sharp}
is negatively graded, any

Par^{\sharp}
-module
V

has the
degree filtration

0=V_{-1}<V_{0}<\cdots<V_{n}<\cdots
defined from
V_{n}:=\bigoplus_{m\leq n}1_{m}V
. The section
V_{n}/V_{n-1}
in this
filtration is isomorphic to
\infl^{\sharp}(1_{n}V)
, viewing
1_{n}V
as a

{S\!ym}
-module by restriction.
It follows that

(3.36)

[V:S^{\sharp}(\lambda)]=[1_{n}V:S(\lambda)]

for
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
.

Theorem 3.8
.

For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{l},\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{m}
and
\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
, we
have that

[S^{\sharp}(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S^{\sharp}(\nu):S^{\sharp}(\lambda)]=\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
.

Proof.

Call
d

admissible
if
0\leq d\leq\min(l+m-n,l+n-m,m+n-l)
and
d\equiv m+n+n\pmod{2}
. For such a
d
,
let
M_{l,m,n}^{d}
be the sub-bimodule of the
(\Bbbk S_{l},\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n})
-bimodule

M_{l,m,n}:=1_{l}\left(\big(\infl^{\sharp}\Bbbk S_{m}\big){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}\big(\infl^{\sharp}\Bbbk S_{n}\big)\right)=1_{l}Par^{\sharp}1_{\star}\otimes_{Par^{\sharp}\boxtimes Par^{\sharp}}\left(\big(\infl^{\sharp}\Bbbk S_{m}\big)\boxtimes\big(\infl^{\sharp}\Bbbk S_{n}\big)\right)

generated by the vector
f^{d}_{l,m,n}\otimes(1\otimes 1)
, where

f^{d}_{l,m,n}
is as in
eq.

3.34
.

lemma

3.5
implies that

M_{l,m,n}=\bigoplus_{\text{admissible $\scriptstyle d$}}M_{l,m,n}^{d}.

Note also that

1_{l}\left(S^{\sharp}(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S^{\sharp}(\nu)\right)\cong M_{l,m,n}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n}}\left(S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)\right)

as
\Bbbk S_{l}
-modules. In view of this and

eq.

3.36
, the number we are trying to compute is equal to

\left[1_{l}\left(S^{\sharp}(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S^{\sharp}(\nu)\right):S(\lambda)\right]=\sum_{\text{admissible $d$}}\left[M_{l,m,n}^{d}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n}}(S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)):S(\lambda)\right].

Let
\widetilde{M}^{d}_{l,m,n}
be the left
\Bbbk S_{l}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n}
-module obtained from the
(\Bbbk S_{l},\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n})
-bimodule
M^{d}_{l,m,n}
by twisting the right actions of
S_{m}
and

S_{n}
into left actions using
\sigma:g\mapsto g^{-1}
.
By the self-duality of Specht modules, we have that

\left[M_{l,m,n}^{d}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{m}\boxtimes\Bbbk S_{n}}(S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)):S(\lambda)\right]=\left[\widetilde{M}^{d}_{l,m,n}:S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)\right].

Now we claim that
\widetilde{M}^{d}_{l,m,n}
is isomorphic to the
module
\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}

from
lemma

3.7
. To see this, recall from the proof of that lemma
that
\Bbbk\Omega_{l,m,n}^{d}
is the permutation module induced from the
trivial representation of the subgroup
L=S_{a}\times S_{b}\times S_{c}\times S_{d}<S_{l}\times S_{m}\times S_{n}
.
It is easy to see from
eq.

3.34
that
L
acts
trivially on the generating vector
f^{d}_{l,m,n}\otimes(1\otimes 1)\in\widetilde{M}^{d}_{l,m,n}
. Hence, there is a surjective
homomorphism

\Bbbk\Omega^{d}_{l,m,n}\twoheadrightarrow\widetilde{M}^{d}_{l,m,n}
. It
is an isomorphism because both of these modules are of dimension

(l!m!n!)/(a!b!c!d!)
.
From the claim, the previous displayed equation and
lemma

3.7
, the problem is
reduced to computing

\sum_{\text{admissible $d$}}[\Bbbk\Omega^{d}_{l,m,n}:S(\lambda)\boxtimes S(\mu)\boxtimes S(\nu)]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}LR^{\lambda}_{\beta,\gamma,\delta}LR^{\mu}_{\alpha,\gamma,\delta^{\prime}}LR^{\nu}_{\alpha,\beta,\delta^{\prime\prime}}G^{\delta}_{\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime}}.

This expression is equal to the reduced Kronecker coefficient

\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
by a theorem of Littlewood

[
L
]
.
∎

3.5.
Grothendieck rings

Next we describe the Grothendieck rings
K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})
and

K_{0}(Par_{t})
.
For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
, let

(3.37)

P^{\sharp}(\lambda):=\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}S(\lambda).

This is a finite-dimensional projective
Par^{\sharp}
-module. In fact, it is the
projective cover of the irreducible
Par^{\sharp}
-module
S^{\sharp}(\lambda)
.
This follows because
P^{\sharp}(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow S^{\sharp}(\lambda)
, and

\End_{Par^{\sharp}}(P^{\sharp}(\lambda))\cong\End_{{S\!ym}}(S(\lambda))\cong\Bbbk
so that
P^{\sharp}(\lambda)
is indecomposable.
Thus,
K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})
is the free
\mathbb{Z}
-module with basis

\big\{[P^{\sharp}(\lambda)]\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}
, and we see that
the monoidal functor
\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}
induces a ring isomorphism

(3.38)

K_{0}({S\!ym})\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}K_{0}(Par^{\sharp}).

Recall from
section

2.6
that
K_{0}({S\!ym})
is identified with the graded ring
\Lambda
of symmetric functions.
Using
eq.

3.38
, it follows that we can also identify
K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})

with
\Lambda
so that
[P^{\sharp}(\lambda)]

corresponds to the Schur function
s_{\lambda}
.
Let

(3.39)

B_{\lambda,\mu}:=\dim\Hom_{Par^{\sharp}}(P^{\sharp}(\mu),P^{\sharp}(\lambda))=[P^{\sharp}(\lambda):S^{\sharp}(\mu)],

i.e.,
(B_{\lambda,\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\in\mathcal{P}}
is
the Cartan matrix of
Par^{\sharp}
.

Lemma 3.9
.

We have that
B_{\lambda,\mu}=\dim e_{\mu}Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}
where
e_{\lambda}\in{S\!ym}
denotes Young’s
idempotent.
Hence:

(i)

B_{\lambda,\lambda}=1
for every
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}
.

(ii)

B_{\lambda,\mu}=0
if
|\mu|>|\lambda|
or
if
|\mu|=|\lambda|
and
\mu\neq\lambda
.

(iii)

If
\lambda=(1^{n})
then

B_{\lambda,\mu}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\text{if $\mu=(1^{n})$ or $\mu=(1^{n-1})$}\\
0&\text{for all other $\mu\in\mathcal{P}$.}\end{array}\right.

Proof.

For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
, the primitive idempotent
e_{\lambda}\in\Bbbk S_{n}
has the property that
S(\lambda)\cong\Bbbk S_{n}e_{\lambda}
. Hence,

P^{\sharp}(\lambda)\cong Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}
.
We deduce that

B_{\lambda,\mu}\mathrel{{\mathop{=}\limits}}\dim\Hom_{Par^{\sharp}}(P^{\sharp}(\mu),P^{\sharp}(\lambda))=\dim\Hom_{Par^{\sharp}}(Par^{\sharp}e_{\mu},Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda})=\dim e_{\mu}Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}.

Parts (i) and (ii) follow easily using this formula.
For (iii), let
\lambda:=(1^{n})
.
Then

e_{\lambda}=\sum_{g\in S_{n}}(-1)^{\ell(g)}g
, so that any crossing
composed with
e_{\lambda}
equals
-e_{\lambda}
.
The space
Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}
is spanned by terms of the form
fe_{\lambda}
for
downward partition diagrams
f\in Par^{\sharp}1_{n}
. When
\lambda=(1^{n})
, it follows using the
anti-symmetry that

fe_{\lambda}=0
if some connected component of
f
is a downward branch
or a downward tree, or if
f
has two components
that are downward leaves. So in this case
Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}
is spanned just
by the vectors
e_{\lambda}
and
(1_{n-1}\star c)e_{\lambda}
where
c
is a single downward leaf. Since these two
elements of
Par^{\sharp}
lie in different weight spaces, they
are linearly independent, so
Par^{\sharp}e_{\lambda}
is
exactly two-dimensional. It remains to observe that
\Bbbk e_{\lambda}
is
the sign representation
S(\lambda)
of
S_{n}
and
\Bbbk(1_{n-1}\star c)e_{\lambda}
is the sign representation
S(\mu)
of
S_{n-1}
for
\mu=(1^{n-1})
.
∎

lemma

3.9
(i)–(ii) shows that the Cartan matrix is unitriangular, hence, invertible.
It follows that the inclusion
Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Proj}}\rightarrow Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
induces an isomorphism

(3.40)

K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp}),

where
K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp})
denotes
the Grothendieck group of the Abelian category

Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
. By
lemma

3.5
, we know that
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
is
biexact on
Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
, so it induces a multiplication making
K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp})

into a ring in such a way that
eq.

3.40
is a ring isomorphism.
Using the isomorphisms
eqs.

3.38
and
3.40
,
the canonical basis
\big\{[S^{\sharp}(\lambda)]\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}
of
K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp})
gives us
another basis
\{\tilde{s}_{\lambda}\>|\>\lambda\in\Lambda\}
for
the ring
\Lambda
.
We call these the
deformed Schur functions
.
We have that

(3.41)

\displaystyle s_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}}B_{\lambda,\mu}\tilde{s}_{\mu},

\displaystyle\tilde{s}_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}}A_{\lambda,\mu}s_{\mu},

where
(B_{\lambda,\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\in\mathcal{P}}
is the Cartan matrix
from
eq.

3.39
and
(A_{\lambda,\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\in\mathcal{P}}
is the inverse matrix.
From the unitriangularity of the latter matrix,
it follows that
\tilde{s}_{\lambda}
is equal to
s_{\lambda}
plus a
linear combination of
s_{\mu}
of strictly lower degree. In other
words, viewing the graded algebra
\Lambda
as a filtered algebra with filtration induced
by the grading, the deformed Schur function
\tilde{s}_{\lambda}
is in
filtered degree
n:=|\lambda|
and
\operatorname{gr}_{n}\tilde{s}_{\lambda}=s_{\lambda}
.
This justifies the name “deformed Schur function”.
By
theorem

3.8
we have that

(3.42)

\tilde{s}_{\mu}\tilde{s}_{\nu}=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}}\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}\tilde{s}_{\lambda},

i.e., the reduced Kronecker coefficients are the structure constants
of
\Lambda
in its inhomogeneous basis
arising from deformed Schur functions.
Comparing with
eq.

2.28
, we deduce that

\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}=LR^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}
if
|\lambda|=|\mu|+|\nu|
and
\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}=0
if
|\lambda|>|\mu|+|\nu|
, both of which are well known properties of reduced Kronecker
coefficients.

Remark 3.10
.

The deformed Schur function
\tilde{s}_{\lambda}\in\Lambda
as just defined is equal to the symmetric function
\tilde{s}_{\lambda}
defined in a different way
[
OZ
]
. This follows from
lemma

3.9
(iii),

eq.

3.42
and the characterization given in
[
OZ
, Th. 1(3)]
.

It remains to pass from
K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})
to
K_{0}(Par_{t})
.
Let
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})
be
the Grothendieck group of the exact category
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
.
It is the free Abelian group on basis

\big\{[\Delta(\lambda)]\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}
.
The following result implies that
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})
is a ring with multiplication induced by

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
.

Theorem 3.11
.

For
V,W\in Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
, we have that

\Tor^{Par_{t}}_{i}(V,W)=0
for all
i>0
, hence,

{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
is biexact on
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
.
For
\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}
, there is a filtration

0=V_{-1}<V_{0}<\cdots<V_{|\mu|+|\nu|}=\Delta(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}\Delta(\nu)
such that

V_{i}/V_{i-1}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{i}}\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus\overline{G}_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}}

where
\overline{G}_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}
is the reduced Kronecker coefficient.

Proof.

The first statement is
[
SS2
, Cor. 6.6]
, which is deduced from

[
SS2
, Props. 4.31–4.32]
using also
the exactness of
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
on
Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}

established in
lemma

3.5

together with exactness of the monoidal functor

\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}
.
The second statement follows by applying

\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}
to the degree filtation of

S^{\sharp}(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}S^{\sharp}(\nu)
, using
theorem

3.8
which computes
the multiplicities.
∎

Now consider the following commutative diagram of rings and ring
homomorphisms, with maps
induced by the indicated biexact monoidal functors:

(3.43)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda\cong K_{0}({S\!ym})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{0}(Par_{t})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t}).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{inc}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par^{\sharp}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par_{t}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{inc}}

(Recall
K_{0}
is the split Grothendieck group
of finitely generated projectives,
K_{0}^{\prime}(Par^{\sharp})
is the Grothendieck
group of the Abelian category
Par^{\sharp}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
,
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})

is the Grothendieck group of the exact category
Par_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{\Delta}}}
,
and all of these Grothendieck groups are actually rings with multiplication induced by
{\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}
.)

Theorem 3.12
.

All of the arrows in
eq.

3.43
are isomorphisms, so that
all of the Grothendieck rings in this diagram are identified with

\Lambda
.

Proof.

We already established this for the top two arrows in
eqs.

3.38
and
3.40
. It is immediate for the arrow on the right since it
takes basis element
[S^{\sharp}(\lambda)]
to basis element

[\Delta(\lambda)]
. The fact that the bottom arrow is an isomorphism
is a general property of upper finite highest weight
categories. Indeed, we have that

(3.44)

[P(\lambda)]=[\Delta(\lambda)]+\text{(a sum of $[\Delta(\mu)]$ for
$\mu$ with $|\mu|<|\lambda|$)},

equality in
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})
. Hence, the transition matrix between
the image of the canonical basis for
K_{0}(Par_{t})
and the standard
basis for
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})
is
invertible, as required to see that the bottom map is an isomorphism.
We deduce that the other two arrows are isomorphisms too using the
commutativity of the diagram.
∎

From
theorem

3.12
,
we see that there are
three
natural basis for

K_{0}(Par_{t})
:

•

The canonical basis
\big\{[P(\lambda)]\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}
arising from the indecomposable projectives.

•

The basis

\big\{[\Delta(\lambda)\>\big|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}
arising from the
standard basis for
K_{0}^{\prime\prime}(Par_{t})
via the isomorphism that is the
bottom arrow of
eq.

3.43
.

•

The basis
\big\{[Q(\lambda)]\>|\>\lambda\in\mathcal{P}\big\}

where

Q(\lambda):=\ind_{{S\!ym}}^{Par_{t}}S(\lambda)\cong\ind_{\mathpzc{Par}^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}S^{\sharp}(\lambda)
.

Note
Q(\lambda)
is a finitely generated projective
Par_{t}
-module which is usually
decomposable. In fact

(3.45)

Q(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)\oplus\text{(a finite direct sum of
$P(\mu)$ for $\mu$ with $|\mu|<|\lambda|$)},

as follows from
eq.

3.44
and the following lemma.

Lemma 3.13
.

For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{n}
, the
Par_{t}
-module
V:=Q(\lambda)
has a filtration

0=V_{-1}<V_{0}<\cdots<V_{n}=V
such that

V_{i}/V_{i-1}\cong\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{i}}\Delta(\mu)^{\oplus B_{\lambda,\mu}}.

In particular,
V_{n}/V_{n-1}\cong\Delta(\lambda)
.

Proof.

Recalling the definition
eq.

3.39
, this follows by applying the exact functor

\ind_{Par^{\sharp}}^{Par_{t}}
to the degree filtration of
P^{\sharp}(\lambda)
,
also using
lemma

3.9
.
∎

Under the identification of
K_{0}(Par_{t})
with
\Lambda
,
the isomorphism classes
[Q(\lambda)]
correspond
to the Schur functions
s_{\lambda}\in\Lambda
,
and the isomorphism classes

[\Delta(\lambda)]
correspond to the deformed Schur functions

\tilde{s}_{\lambda}
. These statements are both clear from
our previous discussion of
K_{0}(Par^{\sharp})
.
The
Q
and
\Delta
bases for
K_{0}(Par_{t})
are independent of the value of the parameter
t
,
whereas the
P
basis coming from indecomposable projectives
undoubtedly does depend on
t
.
For values of
t
such that

Par_{t}
is semisimple (see
corollary

5.11
below), we have that
P(\lambda)=\Delta(\lambda)=\nabla(\lambda)=L(\lambda)
, and
theorem

3.11
implies that

(3.46)

\Delta(\mu){\medcirc\hskip-6.25958pt\star\hskip 1.42262pt}\Delta(\nu)\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}}\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus\overline{G}^{\lambda}_{\mu,\nu}}.

This was established before in
[
E-A
]
;
see also
[
CO
, Lem 5.14]
and

[
BDVO
, Cor. 3.2.2]
.

4.
Jucys-Murphy elements via the affine partition category

Next, we introduce an auxiliary monoidal category
\mathpzc{APar}
, the
affine partition category
. We define this as a
certain monoidal subcategory of the Heisenberg category
\mathpzc{Heis}
,
exploiting an observation of Likeng and Savage from
[
LSR
]
.
We then use
\mathpzc{APar}
to give a new approach to the definition of
the Jucys-Murphy elements of
Par_{t}
.
These were first defined in the context of the partition algebra
by Halverson and Ram
[
HR
]
and computed recursively by Enyang
[
E1
]
.
We also construct more general central elements.

4.1.
Schur-Weyl duality

Recall the generators and relations for the partition category from
definition

3.1
.
The following theorem of Deligne will play a key role in this section;
see e.g.
[
C
, Th. 2.3]
for a proof.

Furthermore, the linear map
\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n,m)\to\Hom_{\Bbbk S_{t}}(U_{t}^{\otimes n},U_{t}^{\otimes m}),f\mapsto\psi_{t}(f)
is an isomorphism whenever
t\geq m+n
.

For the next corollary, we assume some basic facts
about semisimplification of monoidal categories;
e.g., see
[
BEEO
, Sec. 2]
which gives a concise summary of everything
needed here.

Corollary 4.2
.

When
t\in\mathbb{N}
, the
functor
\psi_{t}
induces a monoidal equivalence
\overline{\psi}_{t}
between the
semisimplification of
\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})
and
\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
.
In particular,
Par_{t}
is not a semisimple locally unital algebra
in these cases.

Proof.

The functor
\psi_{t}
extends canonically to a functor

\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})\rightarrow\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
. It is well known that
every irreducible

\Bbbk S_{t}
-module appears as a constituent of some tensor power of
U_{t}
, hence, this functor is dense. Now
the first statement follows from the fullness of the functor
\psi_{t}
using

[
BEEO
, Lem. 2.6]
; see also
[
D
, Th. 2.18]
and
[
CO
, Th. 3.24]
.
Since
\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})
has infinitely many isomorphism classes of irreducible objects, it is definitely not equivalent to its semisimplification

\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
. This shows that
\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})
is not a semisimple Abelian category as it
contains non-zero negligible morphisms. Equivalently, the path algebra

Par_{t}
is not semisimple in these cases.
∎

Remark 4.3
.

Continue to assume that
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
By the general theory of semisimplification,
the irreducible objects in the semisimplification of
\Kar(\mathpzc{Par}_{t})

correspond to the indecomposable projective
Par_{t}
-modules
P(\lambda)

of non-zero categorical dimension. In
[
D
, Prop. 6.4]
, Deligne showed
that
P(\lambda)
has non-zero categorical dimension if and only if
t-|\lambda|>\lambda_{1}-1
, in which case the irreducible
object of the semisimpliciation arising from
P(\lambda)
corresponds
under the equivalence
\overline{\psi}_{t}

to the irreducible
\Bbbk S_{t}
-module
S(\kappa)

where
\kappa:=(t-|\lambda|,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots)
.

The
generic partition category

\mathpzc{Par}
is the strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category with the same generating object and generating morphisms as
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
subject to all of the same relations except for the
final relation in
eq.

3.6
, which is omitted. The morphism

(4.1)

T:=\hbox to16.11pt{\vbox to28.18pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 8.05525pt\lower-5.55522pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 1.97 L 0 21.65}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

is strictly central in
\mathpzc{Par}
, so that

\mathpzc{Par}
can be viewed as a

\Bbbk[T]
-linear monoidal category.
For
t\in\Bbbk
, let

(4.2)

\operatorname{ev}_{t}:\mathpzc{Par}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

be the canonical functor taking
T
to
t1_{\mathbbm{1}}
.
Using the basis theorem for
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
for infinitely many values of
t
,
one obtains a basis theorem for the generic partition category:
each morphism space

\Hom{Par}(n,m)
is free as a
\Bbbk[T]
-module
with basis given by a set of representatives for the equivalence classes of
m\times n
partition diagrams.
From this, we see that
\operatorname{ev}_{t}
induces an isomorphism

\Bbbk\otimes_{\Bbbk[T]}\mathpzc{Par}\cong\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
,
where on the left hand side we are viewing
\Bbbk
as a
\Bbbk[T]
-module so that
T
acts as
t
.
This point of view is often useful since it can be used to
prove a statement involving relations in

\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
for all values of
t
just by checking it for all sufficiently large positive integers, in which case
theorem

4.1
can often be applied to reduce to a question about
symmetric groups.
To make a precise statement, let

(4.3)

\phi_{t}:=\psi_{t}\circ\operatorname{ev}_{t}:\mathpzc{Par}\rightarrow\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}},

assuming
t\in\mathbb{N}
.

Lemma 4.4
.

If
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}}(n,m)
satifies
\phi_{t}(f)=0

for infinitely many values of
t\in\mathbb{N}

then
f=0
.

Proof.

We can write
f=\sum_{i}p_{i}(T)f_{i}
for polynomials

p_{i}(T)\in\Bbbk[T]
and
f_{i}
running over a set of representatives for the equivalence classes of
m\times n
partition diagrams.
Since
\phi_{t}(f)=0
we have that
\sum_{i}p_{i}(t)\phi_{t}(f_{i})=0
for infinitely many values of
t
. By the final assertion in
theorem

4.1
, this implies
that
\sum_{i}p_{i}(t)\operatorname{ev}_{t}(f_{i})=0
for infinitely many values of
t\geq m+n
.
By the basis theorem in
\mathpzc{Par}_{t}
, this means for each
i
that
p_{i}(t)=0
for infinitely many values of
t
.
Hence,
p_{i}(T)=0
for each
i
.
∎

We note that the proof of
lemma

4.4
depends on our standing assumption that the ground field
\Bbbk

is of characteristic zero.

We refer to the morphisms in
eq.

4.18

as the
left dot
and the
right dot
, and the morphisms in
eq.

4.19
as the
left crossing
and the
right crossing
, respectively.
The other shorthands for the generating morphisms of
\mathpzc{APar}
introduced in
definition

4.6

are the same as the
symbols used for generators of the partition category. This is deliberate, indeed, the morphisms
eqs.

4.15
,
4.16
and
4.17
generate a copy of the generic partition category
\mathpzc{Par}
as a monoidal subcategory of
\mathpzc{Heis}
. This important
observation is due to Likeng and Savage; see
corollary

4.16
below. For now, we just need the following, which is proved in
[
LSR
]
by a direct calculation using the defining relations in
\mathpzc{Heis}
.

Lemma 4.7

(
[
LSR
, Th. 4.1]
)
.

There is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear
monoidal functor

(4.20)

i:\mathpzc{Par}\rightarrow\mathpzc{APar}

sending the generating object and generating morphisms of
\mathpzc{Par}
to the generating object and generating morphisms in
\mathpzc{APar}
denoted by the same diagrams.

Because of the symmetry of the generators of
\mathpzc{APar}

under rotation through
180^{\circ}
, the strictly pivotal structure on
\mathpzc{Heis}
restricts to a strictly pivotal structure on
\mathpzc{APar}
. The left and right dots are duals,
as are the left and right crossings.
Moreover, the cap and the cup making
\boldsymbol{|}
into a self-dual object are given by the same formula
eq.

3.7
as we had before in
\mathpzc{Par}
, hence,
i
is a pivotal monoidal functor.

Finally, to prove
eq.

4.26
, the second set of relations follows from the first set of relations by composing on the bottom with a crossing and using
eq.

4.25
.
For the first set of relations, it suffices to prove the first equality, the second then follows by duality.
Expanding both of the left crossings as morphisms in
\mathpzc{Heis}
produces a sum of four terms, two of which are zero, so we obtain:

Corollary 4.9
.

As a
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal category, the subcategory
\mathpzc{APar}
of
\mathpzc{Heis}

is generated by the object
\boldsymbol{|}\,
, the five undotted generators

eqs.

4.15
,
4.16
and
4.17
, and the left dot.

Proof.

The relations
eqs.

4.23
and
4.24
together show that the right dot and the left and right crossings may be written in terms of the left dot and the other undotted generating morphisms.
∎

where we commuted the dot past a crossing just in the first term.
These are equal.
To deduce
eq.

4.28
, first apply duality to
eq.

4.27
, i.e., rotate through
180^{\circ}
. Then compose on the top and bottom with a crossing and simplify using relations in
\mathpzc{Par}
together with
eq.

4.25
.

To prove
eq.

4.29
, we rewrite its left hand side, replacing the right crossing with a left dot using
eq.

4.24
, then we apply
eq.

Corollary 4.11
.

As a
\Bbbk
-linear category,
\mathpzc{APar}

has object set
\{\boldsymbol{|}^{\star n}\>|\>n\in\mathbb{N}\}
(which we often identify simply
with
\mathbb{N}
)
and morphisms that are linear combinations of vertical
compositions of morphisms in the image of
i:\mathpzc{Par}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Heis}
together with the morphisms

(4.31)

\cdot
\cdot
\cdot
{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}
{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2}
{\scriptscriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
\bullet

for all
n\geq 1
.

Proof.

In view of
corollary

4.9
, we just need to show that one can obtain the endomorphism
of
n
defined by the left dot on the
m
th string (
m=1,\dots,n
)
by taking a linear combinations of compositions of morphisms in the image of
i
and the given morphism
eq.

4.31
(in which the left dot is on the first string).
This follows by induction on
m
using relations
eq.

4.27
and
eq.

4.24
.
∎

Remark 4.12
.

We have not attempted to formulate or prove a basis theorem for the morphism spaces in
\mathpzc{APar}
.
This is closely related to the problem of finding a complete monoidal presentation for
\mathpzc{APar}
.

4.4.
Action of
\mathpzc{APar}
on
\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}

Suppose that
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
The restriction of the functor
\Theta
from
eq.

4.14
to the subcategory
\mathpzc{APar}
is a strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor

\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}({S\!ym}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}})

sending the generating object
\boldsymbol{|}
to the endofunctor
E\circ F
(induction after restriction).
Since
E\circ F
takes
\Bbbk S_{t}
-modules to
\Bbbk S_{t}
-modules, the restriction of
\Theta
gives strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functors

(4.32)

\Theta_{t}:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}).

The functor
\Theta_{t}
takes

\boldsymbol{|}
to the endofunctor

\ind_{S_{t-1}}^{S_{t}}\circ\res_{S_{t-1}}^{S_{t}}=\Bbbk S_{t}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{t-1}}

of
\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
; this should be interpreted as the zero functor in the case
t=0
.
The natural transformations arising by
applying
\Theta_{t}
to the other generating morphisms of
\mathpzc{APar}
may be
computed using the formulae after
eq.

4.14
(taking
n:=t
). Explicitly, one obtains the following for

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{5.18192pt}{8.02063pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{64}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\!\!\!\right)_{V}

\displaystyle:U_{t}\otimes V\rightarrow U_{t}\otimes V,

\displaystyle u_{i}\otimes v

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{i}\otimes(i\>j)v.

Proof.

There is an isomorphism
\Bbbk S_{t}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{t-1}}\triv_{S_{t-1}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}U_{t},g\otimes 1\mapsto gu_{t}
.
Combining this with the tensor identity, we obtain a natural
\Bbbk S_{t}
-module isomorphism

(4.34)

\displaystyle(\alpha^{(t)}_{1})_{V}:\Bbbk S_{t}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{t-1}}V

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}U_{t}\otimes V,

\displaystyle g\otimes v

\displaystyle\mapsto gu_{t}\otimes gv

for
V\in\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
.
This defines an isomorphism
\alpha^{(t)}_{1}:\Bbbk S_{t}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{t-1}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\Rightarrow}\limits}}U_{t}\otimes
.
Let
\alpha^{(t)}_{n}:=\alpha^{(t)}_{1}\cdots\alpha^{(t)}_{1}
be the
n
-fold horizontal composition of
\alpha^{(t)}_{1}
.
This is a natural isomorphism
\alpha^{(t)}_{n}:(\Bbbk S_{t}\otimes_{\Bbbk S_{t-1}})^{\circ n}\mathrel{{\mathop{\Rightarrow}\limits}}(U\otimes)^{\circ n}
whose value on a
\Bbbk S_{t}
-module
V
is given explicitly by the map

\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{n}\big)_{V}:g_{n}\otimes\cdots\otimes g_{1}\otimes v\mapsto g_{n}u_{t}\otimes g_{n}g_{n-1}u_{t}\otimes\cdots\otimes g_{n}g_{n-1}\cdots g_{1}u_{t}\otimes g_{n}g_{n-1}\cdots g_{1}v.

Now
define

\Phi_{t}:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}})

to be the strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor
taking the object
n
to

(U_{t}\otimes)^{\circ n}
, and defined on a morphism

f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)
by

\Phi_{t}(f):=\alpha^{(t)}_{m}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{n}\big)^{-1}
.
It is immediate from this definition that

\alpha^{(t)}=\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{n}\big)_{n\geq 0}:\Theta_{t}\Rightarrow\Phi_{t}

is an isomorphism of strict
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functors.

It remains to check that
\Phi_{t}
as defined in the previous paragraph is equal to the functor
\Phi_{t}
defined on generating morphisms
in the statement of the lemma. So we need to check for
each generating morphism
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)

that the formula for
\Phi_{t}(f)_{V}
written
in the statement of the lemma is equal to

\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{m}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{n}\big)_{V}^{-1}

for
V\in\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}
and
t\in\mathbb{N}
. This is a routine but lengthy
calculation. We just go through a couple of the cases.

If
f
is the crossing, we need to show that

\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes u_{j}\otimes v)=u_{j}\otimes u_{i}\otimes v
.
Now we consider four cases.
If
t\neq i\neq j\neq t
we have that

\displaystyle\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes u_{j}\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\right)\left((i\>t)\otimes(j\>t)\otimes(j\>t)(i\>t)v\right)

\displaystyle=\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\left((i\>t)(j\>t)\otimes(j\>t)\otimes(i\>t)v\right)=u_{j}\otimes u_{i}\otimes v.

If
i=j
we have that

\displaystyle\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes u_{j}\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\right)\left((i\>t)\otimes 1\otimes(i\>t)v\right)

\displaystyle=\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\left((i\>t)\otimes 1\otimes(i\>t)v\right)=u_{j}\otimes u_{i}\otimes v.

If
i=t\neq j
we have that

\displaystyle\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes u_{j}\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\right)\left(1\otimes(j\>t)\otimes(j\>t)v\right)

\displaystyle=\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\left((j\>t)\otimes(j\>t)\otimes v\right)=u_{j}\otimes u_{i}\otimes v.

Finally if
i\neq t=j
we have that

\displaystyle\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes u_{j}\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\right)\left((i\>t)\otimes(i\>t)\otimes v\right)

\displaystyle=\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{2}\big)_{V}\left(1\otimes(i\>t)\otimes(i\>t)v\right)=u_{j}\otimes u_{i}\otimes v.

This completes the check in this case.

If
f
is the left dot, we have that

\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{1}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\circ\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{1}\big)_{V}^{-1}\right)(u_{i}\otimes v)=\left(\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{1}\big)_{V}\circ\Theta_{t}(f)_{V}\right)\left((i\>t)\otimes(i\>t)v\right)\\
=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\big(\alpha^{(t)}_{1}\big)_{V}((i\>t)(j\>t)\otimes(i\>t)v)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}(i\>t)(j\>t)u_{t}\otimes(i\>t)(j\>t)(i\>t)v.

If
i=t
this is
\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{j}\otimes(j\>t)v
which is right.
If
i\neq t
we pull out the
j=i
and
j=t
terms of the sum, simplify
the three types of terms separately, then recombine
to get the desired expression

\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{j}\otimes(i\>j)v
.
∎

We now have in our hands monoidal functors

\phi_{t}
from
eq.

4.3
,

i
from
eq.

4.20
, and
\Phi_{t}

from
eq.

4.33
. Let

(4.35)

\operatorname{Act}:\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}\rightarrow\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}})

be the
\Bbbk
-linear monoidal functor induced by the Kronecker product, i.e.,

\operatorname{Act}(V)=V\otimes
for a
\Bbbk S_{t}
-module
V

and
\operatorname{Act}(f)=f\otimes
for a homomorphism
f:V\rightarrow V^{\prime}
.

Lemma 4.14
.

For every
t\in\mathbb{N}
, the following diagram
commutes up to the obvious canonical isomorphism of monoidal functors:

(4.36)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathpzc{APar}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathpzc{End}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathpzc{Par}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Bbbk S_{t}{\operatorname{-Mod_{fd}}}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi_{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi_{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{Act}}

Proof.

The composition

\Phi_{t}\circ i
takes the
n
th object of
\mathpzc{APar}
to
(U_{t}\otimes)^{\circ n}
, while
\operatorname{Act}\circ\phi_{t}
takes it to
U_{t}^{\otimes n}\otimes
.
Let

\beta^{(t)}_{n}:(U_{t}\otimes)^{\circ n}\mathrel{{\mathop{\Rightarrow}\limits}}U_{t}^{\otimes n}\otimes

be the canonical isomorphism between these functors defined by associativity of tensor product.
Then

\beta^{(t)}=\big(\beta^{(t)}_{n}\big)_{n\geq 0}:\Phi_{t}\circ i\Rightarrow\operatorname{Act}\circ\phi_{t}
is an isomorphism
of monoidal functors. To see this, we need to check naturality. This follows
because the five formulae defining
\phi_{t}

from
theorem

4.1
tensored on the right with a vector
v

are exactly
the same as the formulae defining
\Phi_{t}
on these five generating morphisms
from
lemma

4.13
.
∎

defined on

Proof.

For
t\in\mathbb{N}
, let
\gamma^{(t)}_{n}:U_{t}^{\otimes n}\otimes\triv_{S_{t}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}U_{t}^{\otimes n}
be the obvious isomorphism
sending

u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}}\otimes 1\mapsto u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}}
.
We say that
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)
is
good
if there exists a morphism
\bar{f}\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}}(n,m)
such that

(4.42)

\phi_{t}(\bar{f})=\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{n}\big)^{-1}

for all
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
If
f
is good, there is a
unique

\bar{f}
such that

eq.

4.42
holds for all
t
.
To see this, suppose that
\bar{f}
and
\bar{f}^{\prime}
both satisfy
eq.

4.42
for all
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then
\phi_{t}(\bar{f})=\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{n}\big)^{-1}=\phi_{t}(\bar{f}^{\prime})
, so that
\phi_{t}(\bar{f}-\bar{f}^{\prime})=0
for all
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
In view of
lemma

4.4
this implies that
\bar{f}=\bar{f}^{\prime}
as claimed.

Suppose that

f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)
and
g\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(l,m)

are both good. Then
f\circ g
is good with
\overline{f\circ g}:=\bar{f}\circ\bar{g}
.
This follows because

\phi_{t}(\bar{f}\circ\bar{g})=\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\big)^{-1}\circ\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{l}\big)^{-1}=\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f\circ g))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{l}\big)^{-1}.

Similarly, sums of good morphisms are good with
\overline{f+g}:=\bar{f}+\bar{g}
.

In this paragraph, we show that every morphism in
\mathpzc{APar}
is good.
In view of the previous paragraph, it suffices to show that some family of generating morphisms for
\mathpzc{APar}
are all good. Hence, in view of
corollary

4.11
,
it is enough to show that
i(f)

is good for every morphism
f
in
\mathpzc{Par}
and that the morphisms
eq.

4.31
are good
for all
n
.
For
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}}(n,m)
, the morphism

i(f)
is good with
\overline{i(f)}:=f
. This follows from the following calculation using
lemma

4.14
:

\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(i(f)))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\big)^{-1}=\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\circ\operatorname{Ev}(\operatorname{Act}(\phi_{t}(f)))\circ\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{m}\big)^{-1}=\phi_{t}(f).

Also the morphism
f
from
eq.

4.31
is good for every
n
.
To see this, let
\bar{f}
be the morphism on the right hand side of
eq.

4.39
. Using the definition in
theorem

4.1
,
\phi_{t}(\bar{f})
is the map

u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}}\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{j}
.
Also using the definition in
lemma

4.13
,
\operatorname{Ev}(\Phi_{t}(f))
is the map

u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}}\otimes 1\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{j}\otimes 1
.
On contracting the final
\otimes 1
using
\gamma^{(t)}_{n}
, these are equal,
as required to prove that
f
is good.

Now we can define a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
p
making
eq.

4.40

commute (up to natural isomorphism) for all
t\in\mathbb{N}
.
On objects, define
p
by declaring that

p(n)=n
for each
n\geq 0
.
On a morphism
f\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)
, we define

p(f):=\bar{f}
. The checks made so far imply that this is a well-defined

\Bbbk
-linear functor satisfying
eq.

4.39
.
The equation
eq.

4.42
shows that

\gamma^{(t)}=\big(\gamma^{(t)}_{n}\big)_{n\geq 1}:\operatorname{Ev}\circ\Phi_{t}\Rightarrow\phi_{t}\circ p
is a natural isomorphism.
We have also already shown that
p\circ i=\Id_{\mathpzc{Par}}

and that
eq.

4.39
holds.
Thus, we have established the existence of a
\Bbbk
-linear functor

p:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}
satisfying all of the properties in the statement of the theorem. The uniqueness of
p
follows from
corollary

4.11
.

It remains to check the three properties
eq.

4.41
.
These can be checked using the commutativity of
eq.

4.40
in the same way as we just established
eq.

4.39
. Alternatively, and possibly quicker, they can be deduced
directly from
eq.

4.39
using the relations
eqs.

4.23
,
4.24
and
4.25
,
respectively. We leave the details to the reader.
∎

The faithfulness of
i
in the
following corollary was already proved in two different ways in
[
LSR
]
.
Our approach is similar in spirit to the first proof given in

loc. cit.
, i.e., the
argument used to prove
[
LSR
, Th. 5.2]
.

Corollary 4.16
.

The functor
i:\mathpzc{Par}\rightarrow\mathpzc{APar}
is faithful
and the functor
p:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}
is full.

Proof.

This follows because
p\circ i=\Id_{\mathpzc{Par}}
.
∎

Corollary 4.17
.

The functor
p
induces an isomorphism

\mathpzc{APar}/\mathcal{I}\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}\mathpzc{Par}
where
\mathcal{I}
is the left tensor ideal of
\mathpzc{APar}
generated by the morphism

Proof.

The left tensor ideal
\mathcal{I}
is the data of subspaces

\mathcal{I}(n,m)
of
\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)

for each
m,n\geq 0
which are closed under vertical composition on the top or bottom with any morphism
and closed under horizontal composition on the left with any morphism.
It is clear from
eq.

4.39

that
p
sends morphisms in
\mathcal{I}
to zero, hence,
p
induces a
\Bbbk
-linear functor

\bar{p}:\mathpzc{APar}/\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}
. This is surjective on objects
and full. To see that it is faithful, suppose that

f+\mathcal{I}(n,m)\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}/\mathcal{I}}(n,m)=\Hom_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n,m)/\mathcal{I}(n,m)

is a morphism sent to zero by
\bar{p}
, hence,
p(f)=0
.
In view of
corollary

4.11
and the definition of
\mathcal{I}
, we may assume that
f=i(\bar{f})
for some
\bar{f}\in\Hom_{\mathpzc{Par}}(n,m)
.
Then
\bar{f}=p(i(\bar{f}))=p(f)=0
, so that
f=i(\bar{f})=0
.
∎

Composing the functor
p:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}

with evaluation at any
t\in\Bbbk
gives a full
\Bbbk
-linear functor

(4.43)

\displaystyle p_{t}:=\operatorname{ev}_{t}\circ p

\displaystyle:\mathpzc{APar}\rightarrow\mathpzc{Par}_{t}

such that

(4.44)

4.5.
Jucys-Murphy elements for partition algebras

Now we can explain how affine partition category is related to the works of
Enyang
[
E1
]
and Halverson-Ram
[
HR
]
.
These are concerned with the
partition algebra
, which
is the endomorphism algebra

(4.46)

P_{n}(t):=\End_{\mathpzc{Par}_{t}}(n)=1_{n}Par_{t}1_{n}.

By analogy, we define the
affine partition algebra
to be

(4.47)

AP_{n}:=\End_{\mathpzc{APar}}(n)=1_{n}APar1_{n}.

Let us denote the elements of
AP_{n}
defined by the
left and right dots on the
j
th string by

X_{j}^{L}
and
X_{j}^{R}

of the
k
th and
(k+1)
th strings by
S_{k}^{L}
and
S_{k}^{R}

are algebraically
independent, so they generate a free polynomial algebra of rank
2n

inside
AP_{n}(t)
;
his follows easily from the basis theorem for morphism spaces

\mathpzc{Heis}
proved in
[
K
]
.
Taking the images of the elements
eqs.

4.48
and
4.49
under the functor
p_{t}
from
eq.

4.43

gives us elements of
P_{n}(t)
denoted

(4.50)

\displaystyle x_{j}^{L}

\displaystyle:=p_{t}(X_{j}^{L}),

\displaystyle x_{j}^{R}

\displaystyle:=p_{t}(X_{k}^{R}),

\displaystyle s_{k}^{L}

\displaystyle:=p_{t}(S_{k}^{L}),

\displaystyle s_{k}^{R}

\displaystyle:=p_{t}(S_{k}^{R}).

The notation here depends
implicitly on the values of
n
and
t
, which should be
clear from the context.
By
eqs.

4.44
and
4.45
, we have that

,

x_{1}^{R}=t
,

and

.

Theorem 4.18
.

Suppose that
t\in\mathbb{N}
and let
\psi_{t}:P_{n}(t)\rightarrow\End_{\Bbbk S_{t}}(U_{t}^{\otimes n})

be the homomorphism induced by the functor
\phi_{t}
from
theorem

4.1
.
The elements
x_{j}^{L},x_{j}^{R},s_{k}^{L},s_{k}^{R}\in P_{n}(t)
satisfy

(4.51)

\displaystyle\psi_{t}(x_{j}^{L})(u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{t}u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{j+1}}\otimes(i\>\;i_{j})\left[u_{i_{j}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{i_{1}}\right],

(4.52)

\displaystyle\psi_{t}(x_{j}^{R})(u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{t}u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{j}}\otimes(i\>\;i_{j})\left[u_{i_{j-1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{i_{1}}\right],

(4.53)

\displaystyle\psi_{t}(s_{k}^{L})(u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}})

\displaystyle=u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{k}}\otimes(i_{k}\>\;i_{k+1})\left[u_{i_{k-1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{i_{1}}\right],

(4.54)

\displaystyle\psi_{t}(s_{k}^{R})(u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{1}})

\displaystyle=u_{i_{n}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{k+2}}\otimes(i_{k}\>\;i_{k+1})\left[u_{i_{k+1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{i_{2}}\otimes u_{i_{1}}\right]

for
1\leq i_{1},\dots,i_{n}\leq t
, where we are using the diagonal action of

S_{t}
on tensor powers of
U_{t}
.

Proof.

This follows from the commutativity of
eq.

4.40
,
eq.

4.50
and the formulae in
lemma

4.13
.
∎

Corollary 4.19
.

Identifying
P_{n}(t)
with the partition algebra in
[
E1
]

by reflecting diagrams through a vertical axis to account for the fact that we number vertices from right to left rather than from left to right,
the elements
eq.

4.50

are related to the elements
L_{\frac{1}{2}},L_{1},\dots
and
\sigma_{\frac{3}{2}},\sigma_{2},\dots
of the partition algebra
P_{n}(t)
defined
in
[
E1
]
according to the dictionary

(4.55)

\displaystyle x_{j}^{L}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow L_{j},

\displaystyle t-x_{j}^{R}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow L_{j-\frac{1}{2}},

\displaystyle s_{k}^{L}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow\sigma_{k+\frac{1}{2}},

\displaystyle s_{k}^{R}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow\sigma_{k+1}.

Hence, by
[
E1
, Th. 5.5]
, the elements
x_{j}^{L}
and
t-x_{j}^{R}

are identified with the Jucys-Murphy elements introduced originally by Halverson and Ram in
[
HR
]
.

Proof.

Enyang’s elements are defined by a recurrence relation which is independent of the value of the parameter
t
. Hence, his elements can be viewed as specializations at
T=t
of corresponding elements of the generic partition algebra
\End_{\mathpzc{Par}}(n)
.
To identify them with our elements, we can use
lemma

4.4
to see that it suffices to check that they act in the same way on
U_{t}^{\otimes n}
for infinitely many values of
the parameter
t\in\mathbb{N}
. This follows on comparing
eqs.

4.51
,
4.52
,
4.53
and
4.54

to the formulae in

[
E1
, Prop. 5.2, Prop. 5.3]
.
∎

Remark 4.20
.

Alternatively, one can prove
corollary

4.19
inductively, using the recurrence relations in
lemma

4.10
which are equivalent to Enyang’s recurrence relations
[
E1
, (3.1)–(3.4)]
. In fact, all of the relations derived in
loc. cit.
can now be deduced easily using the relations in
\mathpzc{APar}
derived in the previous subsection.

Remark 4.21
.

Recently, Creedon
[
Cr
]
has
introduced a renormalization of the Jucys-Murphy elements, which he denotes
by
N_{1},N_{2},\dots,N_{2n}\in P_{n}(t)
. They are defined in terms of the Enyang-Halverson-Ram elements simply by
N_{2j-1}:=L_{j-\frac{1}{2}}-{\textstyle\frac{t}{2}}
and

N_{2j}:=L_{j}-{\textstyle\frac{t}{2}}
.
The dictionary between Creedon’s elements and ours is

(4.56)

\displaystyle x_{j}^{L}-\textstyle{\frac{t}{2}}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow N_{2j},

\displaystyle{\textstyle\frac{t}{2}}-x_{j}^{R}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow N_{2j-1}.

The motivation for such a
renormalization will be discussed further in
remark

4.26
below.

4.6.
Central elements

By the
center
of a
\Bbbk
-linear category
\mathpzc{A}
, we mean the (unital)
commutative algebra

Z(\mathpzc{A}):=\End_{\mathpzc{A}}(\Id_{\mathpzc{A}})
of endomorphisms of the identity endofunctor of
\mathpzc{A}
.
Thus, an element
z\in Z(\mathpzc{A})
is a tuple
(z_{X})_{X\in\operatorname{ob}\mathpzc{A}}
such that

z_{Y}\circ f=f\circ z_{X}
for all morphisms
f:X\rightarrow Y
in
\mathpzc{A}
.
Equivalently, in terms of the path algebra
A
,
it is the algebra

(4.57)

Z(A):=\left\{z=\left(z_{X}\right)_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}\in\prod_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}A1_{X}\>\Bigg|\>za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\right\},

interpreting the products in the obvious way.
We note that there is an algebra isomorphism

(4.58)

\End_{A\boxtimes A^{{\operatorname{op}}}}(A)\mathrel{{\mathop{\rightarrow}\limits}}Z(A),\qquad\zeta\mapsto\left(\zeta(1_{X})\right)_{x\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}\in\prod_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}A1_{X},

where the algebra on the left is
the endomorphism algebra of the

A\boxtimes A^{\operatorname{op}}
-module associated to the

(A,A)
-bimodule
A
.
If
A
is locally finite-dimensional, then it is a locally finite-dimensional

A\boxtimes A^{{\operatorname{op}}}
-module, hence, by
[
BS
, Lem. 2.10]
,
the endomorphism algebra

\End_{A\boxtimes A^{{\operatorname{op}}}}(A)\cong Z(A)
is a
pseudo-compact topological algebra with respect to the pro-finite topology (ideals of finite codimension form a base of neighborhoods of zero).

In the locally finite-dimensional case,
Z(A)
is isomorphic to the algebra
C(A)^{*}
that is the linear dual of the

cocenter

C(A)
. The cocenter is a cocommutative coalgebra isomorphic
to
\operatorname{Coend}_{A\boxtimes A^{{\operatorname{op}}}}(A)
in the notation of
[
BS
, (2.15)]
. To define
C(A)
explicitly, note that the space

D:=\bigoplus_{X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}(1_{X}A1_{Y})^{*}
is naturally an
(A,A)
-bimodule
with
1_{Y}D1_{X}=(1_{X}A1_{Y})^{*}
.
Also each
1_{X}D1_{X}
is a coalgebra as it is the dual of the finite-dimensional algebra
1_{X}A1_{X}
. Hence,

\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}D1_{X}
is a coalgebra. Then the cocenter is

(4.59)

C(A):=\Big(\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}D1_{X}\Big)\Big/J

where
J
is the coideal spanned by the elements

\left\{af-fa\>\big|\>X,Y\in\mathbb{O}_{A},a\in 1_{X}A1_{Y},f\in 1_{Y}D1_{X}\right\}
.
To identify
C(A)^{*}
with
Z(A)
, note that the linear dual of the coalgebra

\bigoplus_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}D1_{X}
is the algebra

\prod_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}A1_{X}
; the annihilator
J^{\circ}

of the coideal
J
defines a subalgebra of

\prod_{X\in\mathbb{O}_{A}}1_{X}A1_{X}

which is exactly the center
Z(A)
according
to the original definition
eq.

4.57
.

In this subsection, we are going to construct a
family of elements

(z^{(r)})_{r\geq 1}

in the center
Z(APar_{t})
of the affine partition category
\mathpzc{APar}_{t}
.

Also introduce the rational function

(4.62)

\alpha_{x}(u):=\frac{(u-(x+1))(u-(x-1))}{(u-x)^{2}}\in\Bbbk(x,u).

The expansion of this as a power series in
\Bbbk[x][\![u^{-1}]\!]

is

(4.63)

\displaystyle\alpha_{x}(u)

\displaystyle=1-(u-x)^{-2}=1-u^{-2}-2xu^{-3}-3x^{2}u^{-4}-4x^{3}u^{-5}-\cdots,

(4.64)

\displaystyle\alpha_{x}(u)^{-1}

\displaystyle=1+u^{-2}+2xu^{-3}+(3x^{2}+1)u^{-4}+(4x^{3}+4x)u^{-5}+\cdots.

∎

Corollary 4.24
.

For each
r\geq 1
, the element
Z^{(r)}=(Z^{(r)}_{n})_{n\geq 0}\in\prod_{n\geq 0}1_{n}APar1_{n}

defined from

Z^{(r)}_{n}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left((X_{i}^{L})^{r}-(X_{i}^{R})^{r}\right)=\left(X_{1}^{L}\right)^{r}+\cdots+\left(X_{n}^{L}\right)^{r}-\left(X_{1}^{R}\right)^{r}-\cdots-\left(X_{n}^{R}\right)^{r}

belongs to
Z(APar)
(notation as in
eqs.

4.48
and
4.49
).
Moreover, the elements
Z^{(1)},Z^{(2)},\dots
generate the same subalgebra

Z_{0}(APar)

of
Z(APar)
as the elements
C^{(3)},C^{(4)},\dots
.

Proof.

Let
f(u):=\alpha_{y}(u)/\alpha_{x}(u)
for short.
Then define
g(u):=f^{\prime}(u)/f(u)=\frac{d}{du}(\ln f(u))
to be its logarithmic derivative.
We have that

\displaystyle g(u)

\displaystyle=\left(-\frac{1}{u-(x-1)}+\frac{2}{u-x}-\frac{1}{u-(x+1)}\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{u-(y-1)}+\frac{2}{u-y}-\frac{1}{u-(y+1)}\right)

\displaystyle=2\cdot 3(y-x)u^{-4}+2\cdot 6(y^{2}-x^{2})u^{-5}+2\cdot[10(y^{3}-x^{3})+5(y-x)]u^{-6}+\cdots.

We deduce for
r\geq 1
that the
u^{-r-3}
-coefficient of
g(u)
is equal to

2\binom{r+2}{2}(y^{r}-x^{r})
plus a linear combination of terms

(y^{s}-x^{s})
for
1\leq s<r
with
s\equiv r\pmod{2}
.

The coefficients of the power series
C^{\prime}(u)/C(u)
are polynomials in the coefficients of the series

C(u)
.
Hence, by the theorem, these coefficients are all central.
To compute them, we
take logarithmic derivatives of
eq.

4.67
to obtain the identity

C^{\prime}_{n}(u)/C_{n}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hbox to63.21pt{\vbox to32.43pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.535pt\lower-9.2669pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
